profile.summary: gLM2 is a genomic language model that reads a stretch of genome as a mixture of two alphabets: protein coding regions as amino acids, and the intergenic sequence between them as nucleotides. Each element is prefixed with a strand token. It is a transformer encoder trained by masked language modelling on the OMG metagenomic corpus, and the authors say its representations carry functional information as well as coevolutionary signals in protein-protein interfaces and genomic regulatory syntax.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: Model Description; model card: Model Description; Europe PMC abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: gLM2 is a transformer encoder trained with the masked language modelling objective. The input is a contig written as alternating coding and intergenic elements: coding elements as uppercase amino acids, intergenic elements as lowercase nucleotides, so the two alphabets cannot collide, and each element prefixed by <+> or <-> for the strand. The 650M checkpoint's config gives depth 33, dimension 1280, 20 heads, a SwiGLU feed-forward and a vocabulary of 37 tokens; the 150M checkpoint's config gives depth 30, dimension 640 and 10 heads. Pretraining used 315B tokens with a context length of 4096. An update in September 2024 raised the context from 2048 to 4096 tokens and changed intergenic tokenisation from BPE to per-nucleotide.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Model Description, UPDATE(09/2024); model card: Model Description, Training Details; config.json

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two checkpoints are published: tattabio/gLM2_150M and tattabio/gLM2_650M. Both cards carry the same September 2024 update note, the same 315B pretraining tokens and the same 4096 context length, and their configs differ in size: depth 33 and dimension 1280 for 650M, depth 30 and dimension 640 for 150M. A result should name which checkpoint was used and its Hugging Face revision, because the September 2024 update changed both the context length and the intergenic tokenisation. This page read the 650M checkpoint at revision 3c4037ae and the 150M checkpoint at revision 93c88529.

strengths.text: Reads genes and the sequence between them in one pass, which the authors say lets it use genomic context to learn functional representations.
strengths.source_locator: README.md: Model Description; Europe PMC abstract

strengths.text: The authors report that the categorical Jacobian of gLM2 predicts an interaction between 2ONK_A (ModA) and 2ONK_C (ModC), where they say ESM2 and Evo predict none.
Code, both checkpoints and the OMG training corpus are all public, with Apache-2.0 licences on the code and weights and no gating.
strengths.source_locator: LICENSE; Hugging Face API; Europe PMC abstract

limitations.text: Input must be prepared, not raw DNA: coding regions have to be called and translated to uppercase amino acids, intergenic sequence kept as lowercase nucleotides, and each element given a strand token. The tokenizer depends on that case and on the strand tokens.
The context is 4096 tokens, so only a short stretch of a genome fits in one pass.
The September 2024 update changed the context length and the intergenic tokenisation, so the checkpoint revision matters when reporting a result.
The published usage example calls .cuda() and loads custom model code with trust_remote_code, so a CUDA GPU is assumed and remote code is executed.

run_guide.summary: Load the gLM2 650M checkpoint and extract embeddings for a short mixed-modality contig.
prerequisites: Python with PyTorch and transformers.
A CUDA GPU: the published example calls .cuda() and loads the weights in bfloat16. Memory needs are not stated in the sources read.
Code and weights are Apache-2.0 and the checkpoints are not gated.
The input must already be split into coding and intergenic elements, with amino acids uppercase and nucleotides lowercase.

steps.title: Install PyTorch and transformers
steps.shell: pip install torch transformers
steps.explanation: The sources name no install command; this line installs the two packages their usage example imports.

steps.title: Extract embeddings for a contig
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained('tattabio/gLM2_650M', torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, trust_remote_code=True).cuda()
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('tattabio/gLM2_650M', trust_remote_code=True)

# A contig with two proteins and an inter-genic sequence.
# NOTE: Nucleotides should always be lowercase, and prepended with `<+>`.
sequence = "<+>MALTKVEKRNRIKRRVRGKISGTQASPRLSVYKSNK<+>aatttaaggaa<->MLGIDNIERVKPGGLELVDRLVAVNRVTKVTKGGRAFGFSAIVVVGNED"

# Tokenize the sequence.
encodings = tokenizer([sequence], return_tensors='pt')

# Extract embeddings.

sections.body: AlphaGenome progressively downsamples DNA with convolutional blocks, then uses a transformer tower and pairwise interaction blocks to represent long-range context. A U-Net-style decoder restores sequence resolution using skip connections. Modality-specific heads predict one-dimensional genomic tracks, splicing outputs and two-dimensional contact maps.

profile.summary: Boltz predicts biomolecular complex structures; Boltz-2 also predicts binding affinity.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Boltz-2 first encodes the molecular inputs, alignments and optional templates into token and pair features. A Pairformer trunk updates those features and conditions atom-coordinate diffusion to generate a complex. Separate confidence and affinity modules assess the prediction; affinity classification and regression outputs answer different questions.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Boltz-1 and Boltz-2 are distinct released generations; the catalogue does not select an evaluated checkpoint. The Boltz-2 report describes training crops up to 768 tokens. This is a training-crop size rather than a universal inference maximum; affinity additionally uses a pocket crop.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Chai-1 predicts the structures of biomolecular complexes containing proteins, nucleic acids and small molecules. An AlphaFold3-like structure architecture dominated by pair-biased self-attention, with additional protein-language-model embeddings and optional inter-chain constraint features. The documented inputs are FASTA sequences, ligand SMILES and optional alignments, templates, contacts or covalent-bond restraints. The output consists of sampled complex structures; the default command produces five predictions.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DNABERT-2 merges recurring DNA substrings into byte-pair tokens, then processes those tokens with a masked-language-model transformer. ALiBi supplies distance-dependent attention biases, while FlashAttention changes how attention is computed. The resulting contextual embeddings need an explicit pooling rule and prediction head for a downstream task.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ESMFold predicts protein structures directly from amino-acid sequence using ESM-2 representations. ESM-2 sequence representations feed a folding trunk and structure module. The checked v1 configuration has 48 trunk blocks, eight structure-module blocks and up to four recycles. The documented inputs are protein amino-acid sequence; the ESMFold interface also accepts chains separated by a colon. The output consists of predicted PDB structure and confidence values.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GEARS predicts transcriptional responses to single- and multi-gene perturbations from single-cell perturbation screens. Two graph encoders represent gene coexpression and Gene Ontology perturbation similarity. Perturbation embeddings are composed with gene embeddings, then a cross-gene network and gene-specific decoders predict expression changes. The documented inputs are single-cell expression data, perturbation labels and the graph resources used by the configured model. The output consists of predicted gene-expression responses and genetic-interaction analyses.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MIMIC represents DNA, RNA, protein and associated molecular measurements in a shared multimodal model. Transformer encoder-decoder: 20 encoder layers and 12 decoder layers, width 1,536, rotary positional embeddings, mixed attention and five register tokens. The documented inputs are co-observed molecular modalities and optional text context, grouped into nucleic, protein and text tracks. The output consists of embeddings or generated modalities, such as residue solvent accessibility or splice-site classes.

sections.body: Pangolin predicts splice-site strength and changes caused by genetic variants. Dilated convolutional network with 16 residual blocks and skip connections; separate probability and usage outputs for heart, liver, brain and testis. The documented inputs are VCF or CSV variants, reference FASTA and matching gene annotations; custom sequence inference is also available. The output consists of predicted increases/decreases in splice-site strength and their positions.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProkBERT is a family of microbial DNA encoders used for sequence representation, promoter prediction and phage identification. MegatronBERT-based encoder using local-context-aware k-mer tokenization, learned relative key/value positions and masked-language pretraining. The documented inputs are microbial DNA segments tokenized with the selected variant. The output consists of sequence representations or predictions from separately fine-tuned promoter/phage heads.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: ProkBERT-mini (6-mer, shift 1), mini-c (single base), mini-long (6-mer, shift 2), plus promoter/phage fine-tunes. The paper reports maximum sequence lengths of 1,024bp for mini and 2,048bp for mini-long; tokenization stride distinguishes the variants.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProteinMPNN converts a supplied backbone into a graph whose edges encode interatomic distances. Message-passing layers update node and edge features, and an autoregressive decoder samples amino acids while conditioning on the backbone and previously assigned residues. Fixed residues, tied positions and chain choices change the design task and must accompany its result.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RhoFold+ predicts RNA three-dimensional structures from RNA sequence with alignment information. RNA-FM embeddings and MSA representations enter the Rhoformer transformer stack; a geometry-aware invariant-point-attention structure module predicts frames and torsion angles with recycling. The documented inputs are RNA FASTA (A, U, G, C), optionally a supplied MSA; an MSA is otherwise generated by the full workflow. The output consists of three-dimensional PDB models, predicted distograms, secondary structure and per-residue confidence.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RNA-FM converts an RNA sequence into one token per nucleotide. Twelve transformer encoder blocks use self-attention to produce a 640-dimensional representation at each position. During pretraining, the model learns to recover masked nucleotides from their surrounding sequence. The resulting representations can be supplied to a separately specified downstream model; they are not, by themselves, a structure or functional prediction.

sections.body: The nucleotide-based rna_fm_t12 and codon-based mrna_fm_t12 interfaces are distinct. The original RNA-FM paper sets a training input-length limit of 1,024 and describes a usable limit of 1,022 nucleotides. That limit should not be assigned to mRNA-FM without checking its separate configuration.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: scFoundation embeds gene identity and continuous expression together with source and target read-depth indicators. Its encoder processes only nonzero, unmasked genes. Those contextual embeddings are combined with zero and mask embeddings before a Performer decoder predicts expression across the full gene vocabulary. Pooled encoder outputs represent cells; decoder outputs provide gene-level context.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SpliceAI reads one-hot-encoded DNA through dilated convolutional residual blocks. Skip connections combine features at different depths, and a softmax layer assigns acceptor, donor or neither probabilities to the central positions. The 10kb version requires 5kb of sequence on each side of a scored position; variant scoring compares the reference and alternate predictions.
sections.source_locator: Jaganathan et al., Cell 2019, STAR Methods: SpliceAI architecture and Model training and testing (pp. e2–e3); README.md: usage and License

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper studies 80nt, 400nt, 2kb and 10kb receptive spans. Variant scoring averages five independently trained models; these are not five different assay results. SpliceAI-10k uses 5,000 flanking bases on each side. An input of length l + 10,000 produces predictions for l central positions; receptive span is distinct from maximum input length.
sections.source_locator: Jaganathan et al., Cell 2019, STAR Methods: SpliceAI architecture and Model training and testing (pp. e2–e3); README.md: usage and License

name: AlphaFold 3
description: Biomolecular complex structure prediction

attributes.access: official_source_linked

profile.summary: AlphaFold 3 predicts three-dimensional structures of complexes containing proteins, nucleic acids and other molecular components. It combines a Pairformer representation network with an atomic-coordinate diffusion model. This entry describes the model and local implementation; the hosted AlphaFold Server has a separate profile.
profile.summary_source_locator: Abstract; Model architecture; README: Installation and Usage

sections.title: Joint structure prediction
sections.body: Sequence, chemical and evolutionary features feed a Pairformer, which builds representations of individual tokens and their relationships. A diffusion module then predicts atomic coordinates. Separate heads estimate confidence. The paper describes 48 Pairformer blocks; the architecture models complexes jointly rather than treating every partner as a separately folded structure.
sections.source_locator: Main text: Model architecture; Fig. 1d and Fig. 2

sections.title: Training and evaluation context
sections.body: The standard model uses a structural training cutoff of 30 September 2021. The dedicated PoseBusters Methods section reports a separate model with a 30 September 2019 cutoff, although other training passages disagree (see limitations). Model seeds, templates, input information and ranking also affect the reported comparison; paper evaluation variants are not automatically identical to current downloadable weights.
sections.source_locator: Main paper Methods: Training regime, Inference regime and PoseBusters; supplement Section 5.2

sections.title: Local access
sections.body: The pinned repository provides inference code and a direct Google-hosted weights download. Its README is more current on access than the server FAQ, which still describes an application form. Code and model parameters have different licences; the server output terms should not be substituted for the local weights terms.
sections.source_locator: README: Obtaining Model Parameters and Licences; LICENSE; weights terms: Key things to know; FAQ: model access

sections.title: Training data and provenance
sections.body: Training combines experimental PDB structures with approximately 41 million predicted protein monomers, about 25,000 disorder-focused protein complexes and about 65,000 predicted RNA structures. The supplement also lists transcription-factor examples used during fine-tuning. Its sequence-search resources include UniRef90, UniProt, BFD/Uniclust30, MGnify, Rfam and RNAcentral. These resources have different versions and dates: the structural training cutoff is not a cutoff for every sequence database.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DNABERT-2 merges recurring DNA substrings into byte-pair tokens, then processes those tokens with a masked-language-model transformer. ALiBi supplies distance-dependent attention biases, while FlashAttention changes how attention is computed. The resulting contextual embeddings need an explicit pooling rule and prediction head for a downstream task.

profile.summary: DreaMS learns molecular representations from tandem mass spectra using self-supervised learning.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: DreaMS neural network architecture and Hyperparameters, ablation studies, implementation details and benchmarking; README.md: models/data links; Zenodo record 10997887 metadata.license and files; DreaMS paper Introduction and GeMS mining methods

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DreaMS learns molecular representations from tandem mass spectra using self-supervised learning. PeakEncoder maps spectral peaks to continuous features; SpectrumEncoder uses transformer blocks; a task-specific PeakDecoder maps the contextual features to predictions. The documented inputs are MS/MS spectra with the required peak and acquisition information. The output consists of spectrum embeddings or predictions from separately fine-tuned spectral tasks.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ESM-2 tokenizes an amino-acid sequence and uses a transformer encoder trained to recover masked residues. Self-attention lets each residue representation depend on its sequence context. The released model returns token probabilities and embeddings; a specified pooling rule, task head or complete folding pipeline is needed for a particular biological prediction.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ESMFold predicts protein structures directly from amino-acid sequence using ESM-2 representations. ESM-2 sequence representations feed a folding trunk and structure module. The checked v1 configuration has 48 trunk blocks, eight structure-module blocks and up to four recycles. The documented inputs are protein amino-acid sequence; the ESMFold interface also accepts chains separated by a colon. The output consists of predicted PDB structure and confidence values.
sections.source_locator: ESM README: ESMFold Structure Prediction; official facebook/esmfold_v1 model card and config.json esmfold_config

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: esmfold_v0 and esmfold_v1; v1 is the repository recommendation. Inference length is constrained by memory; the repository documents chunking and CPU offload. Backbone position settings do not alone establish the full folding pipeline limit.
sections.source_locator: ESM README: ESMFold Structure Prediction; official facebook/esmfold_v1 model card and config.json esmfold_config

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GEARS predicts transcriptional responses to single- and multi-gene perturbations from single-cell perturbation screens. Two graph encoders represent gene coexpression and Gene Ontology perturbation similarity. Perturbation embeddings are composed with gene embeddings, then a cross-gene network and gene-specific decoders predict expression changes. The documented inputs are single-cell expression data, perturbation labels and the graph resources used by the configured model. The output consists of predicted gene-expression responses and genetic-interaction analyses.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Nucleotide Transformer is a family of DNA encoders pretrained on human or multispecies sequence corpora. Encoder-only transformers with 6-mer tokens; v1 uses learned positional encodings and v2 uses rotary positions and SwiGLU. The documented inputs are DNA sequences tokenized into 6-mers, with single-base handling of N and remainder bases. The output consists of contextual representations used in specified downstream prediction workflows.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Pangolin predicts splice-site strength and changes caused by genetic variants. Dilated convolutional network with 16 residual blocks and skip connections; separate probability and usage outputs for heart, liver, brain and testis. The documented inputs are VCF or CSV variants, reference FASTA and matching gene annotations; custom sequence inference is also available. The output consists of predicted increases/decreases in splice-site strength and their positions.

profile.summary: ProteinMPNN designs amino-acid sequences for a supplied protein backbone.
profile.summary_source_locator: ProteinMPNN paper: main-text model development; training/README.md: multi-chain training set, list.csv and cluster manifests; protein_mpnn_utils.py: ProteinMPNN; Supplementary Materials: Methods for training multi-chain models / Training data

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProteinMPNN converts a supplied backbone into a graph whose edges encode interatomic distances. Message-passing layers update node and edge features, and an autoregressive decoder samples amino acids while conditioning on the backbone and previously assigned residues. Fixed residues, tied positions and chain choices change the design task and must accompany its result.

profile.summary: RNA-FM learns contextual representations of RNA nucleotides for downstream RNA analyses.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RNA-FM converts an RNA sequence into one token per nucleotide. Twelve transformer encoder blocks use self-attention to produce a 640-dimensional representation at each position. During pretraining, the model learns to recover masked nucleotides from their surrounding sequence. The resulting representations can be supplied to a separately specified downstream model; they are not, by themselves, a structure or functional prediction.

sections.body: The nucleotide-based rna_fm_t12 and codon-based mrna_fm_t12 interfaces are distinct. The original RNA-FM paper sets a training input-length limit of 1,024 and describes a usable limit of 1,022 nucleotides. That limit should not be assigned to mRNA-FM without checking its separate configuration.

profile.summary: SpliceAI annotates sequence variants with predicted splice acceptor and donor changes.
profile.summary_source_locator: Jaganathan et al., Cell 2019, STAR Methods: SpliceAI architecture and Model training and testing (pp. e2–e3); README.md: usage and License

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SpliceAI reads one-hot-encoded DNA through dilated convolutional residual blocks. Skip connections combine features at different depths, and a softmax layer assigns acceptor, donor or neither probabilities to the central positions. The 10kb version requires 5kb of sequence on each side of a scored position; variant scoring compares the reference and alternate predictions.
sections.source_locator: Jaganathan et al., Cell 2019, STAR Methods: SpliceAI architecture and Model training and testing (pp. e2–e3); README.md: usage and License

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper studies 80nt, 400nt, 2kb and 10kb receptive spans. Variant scoring averages five independently trained models; these are not five different assay results. sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SweetNet predicts glycan properties and produces learned representations from glycan graphs. Graph convolutional network; the inspected implementation has three graph-convolution layers, global mean pooling and fully connected prediction layers. profile.summary: Enchant v3 is Iambic's multimodal transformer for drug discovery. It predicts molecular properties and preclinical and clinical endpoints from structures, sequences, omics, assay data, text and images, and Iambic uses it to choose compounds and prioritise experiments.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A mixture-of-experts transformer trained jointly on many data types and endpoints, so that data on one endpoint or molecule informs predictions for related ones. Each prediction carries an uncertainty estimate, which Iambic uses to decide which experiments to run. The model is fine-tuned each week on new laboratory data.
sections.source_locator: enchant-v3-20261102-source-report: 'Leverage model scale', 'Convert model outputs into probability-guided decisions', 'How Enchant impacts discovery at Iambic', 'Enchant v3: Achieving scalable predictability'

sections.title: Versions
sections.body: Enchant v1 (2024) had 1 billion parameters and Enchant v2 (2025) 7 billion. Enchant v3 has 41 billion. New in v3: inverse design, omics-based and image-based prediction, and peptides. profile.summary: Carbon-X is a 14.8 billion parameter chat language model that reads DNA and English in the same conversation. You paste raw DNA into a message and ask a question; it answers in English, for example whether a mutation is likely benign or pathogenic, which organism group a sequence comes from, or what the next bases are. It was built from the general-purpose Qwen3-14B model by adding DNA tokens and further training on DNA and biology text.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: Model Summary; Vocabulary extension

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DNA and text share one token stream in one decoder, with no separate DNA encoder. A hybrid tokeniser keeps Qwen3's BPE vocabulary for text and encodes DNA as non-overlapping 6-mers, so one DNA token covers 6 base pairs; runs of at least 6 A, C, G or T bases are tagged as DNA automatically. Training had four stages. New DNA embeddings were first trained for about 10B tokens with the transformer frozen. The full model was then mid-trained on 302B tokens at sequence length 8,192, a mixture of 55% raw DNA, 20% English, 15% biology text and 10% instruction data. Supervised fine-tuning followed (3 epochs over 20 dataset subsets), then two rounds of GRPO reinforcement learning with code-checked rewards, all with thinking disabled.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Model Summary; Tokenizer; Training (Vocabulary extension, Mid-training, Supervised fine-tuning, Reinforcement learning)

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The released model is HuggingFaceBio/Carbon-X; this page read revision 17de8916. The training pipeline names two intermediate models, Carbon-X-Base (after mid-training) and Carbon-X-SFT (after fine-tuning), and GGUF quantisations exist for llama.cpp. All reported results used thinking disabled and the sampling defaults in generation_config.json (temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20), so a result should name the revision, the model variant and any change to these settings. The training recipes, decontamination scripts and evaluation tasks are in the huggingface/carbon repository.

strengths.text: Asks and answers in plain language, so one model covers variant effect questions, sequence classification and next-base prediction without task-specific heads.
Runs locally on a single 80 GB GPU in bfloat16, with vLLM serving documented, so sensitive sequences can stay on the user's own hardware.

strengths.text: By the developers' own evaluation, it averages 66.7% over five DNA benchmarks with thinking disabled, 27 points above its Qwen3-14B starting point.
Weights and code are Apache-2.0, and the training recipes and the scripts that decontaminate training data against the evaluation benchmarks are public.
strengths.source_locator: Model card: License. LICENSE. carbon-x README: Layout

limitations.text: Not clinically validated; the developers say it should not be used for medical decisions.
Needs a GPU with about 80 GB of memory for the full bfloat16 weights, and Transformers v5 or later.
limitations.source_locator: Model card: How to use; agent section

limitations.text: Can miscount bases, confuse coordinates and invent a sequence's identity when context is missing. Splice-site and histone-mark questions remain weak (29.8% and 34.6% on GenomeQA).
Not trained to design sequences; quality degrades for long DNA generation. Ambiguous bases such as N collapse a whole 6-mer into one <oov> token.

run_guide.summary: Install Transformers, load Carbon-X in bfloat16 on a GPU and ask it whether a variant is likely benign or pathogenic.
prerequisites: A CUDA GPU; the card says the weights fit on a single 80 GB GPU in bfloat16.
Transformers v5 or later, and PyTorch.
Hugging Face Hub access on first load (the tokeniser downloads its BPE vocabulary). The tokeniser is custom code loaded with trust_remote_code=True.
Weights and code are Apache-2.0 and not gated.

steps.title: Install
steps.shell: pip install -U transformers
steps.explanation: The model card's install command. The card requires Transformers v5 or later.

steps.title: Ask a variant question
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

model_id = "HuggingFaceBio/Carbon-X"

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="cuda")

messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": (
            "Reference: ATGGTGCATCTGACTCCTGAGGAGAAGTCTGCCGTTACTGCCCTGTGGGGCAAGG\n"
            "Variant:   ATGGTGCATCTGACTCCTGTGGAGAAGTCTGCCGTTACTGCCCTGTGGGGCAAGG\n\n"
            "Is this variant likely to be benign or pathogenic? Explain your reasoning."
        ),
    }
]
inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    enable_thinking=False,
    return_tensors="pt",
    return_dict=True,
).to(model.device)

outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024)
print(tokenizer.decode(outputs[0][inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True))
PY
steps.explanation: The model card's Python example, unchanged, wrapped in a shell heredoc. It downloads the weights on first run and keeps thinking disabled, as the developers recommend.

outputs: The model's English answer on whether the variant is likely benign or pathogenic, with its reasoning, printed to the terminal. Sampling uses the defaults in generation_config.json, so the text can differ between runs.
limitations: These commands were read from the model card and have not been executed by Rewire.
The snippet does not pin a Hugging Face revision; this page was written from revision 17de89165e25c49e7de4f845d0e5d464469de359.
The card also documents serving with vLLM (vllm serve HuggingFaceBio/Carbon-X --trust-remote-code) behind an OpenAI-compatible API.

name: CodonBERT
description: BERT-style language model of mRNA coding sequences at codon resolution.

attributes.source_locator: Reference 124 in the SI (Li et al.); SI A.3.11 ('BERT-style model focused on codon usage')

version.note: Family record; the checkpoint is on the configuration

profile.summary: CodonBERT is a language model for the coding regions of mRNA, built by Sanofi for mRNA vaccine and therapeutic design. It reads a coding sequence codon by codon and outputs an embedding for each codon. These embeddings can be fine-tuned to predict properties such as protein expression and mRNA degradation, to help choose among the many mRNA sequences that encode the same protein.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results (first paragraph)

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CodonBERT is a BERT model of 12 bidirectional transformer encoder layers, each with 12 attention heads and hidden size 768. Each codon is one token: five symbols (A, U, G, C, N) in three positions give 125 codons, plus five special tokens, for a vocabulary of 130. The input is a pair of sequences joined by a separator, embedded with codon, position and segment embeddings. Pretraining combined two tasks: masked language modelling over codons, and sequence taxonomy prediction, in which the model predicts whether the two sequences come from the same one of 14 taxonomic categories. For downstream tasks, the embeddings feed additional trainable layers.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Model architecture'; Results

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One pretrained PyTorch model is released, as a single zip file (CodonBERT.zip, 954,923,856 bytes, last modified 8 May 2024) on a Sanofi download server rather than a versioned model hub, so the file has no revision identifier beyond its date. The repository holds pretraining and fine-tuning scripts, the NCBI IDs of all 10 million pretraining sequences, a held-out evaluation set, and the downstream datasets including an internal Sanofi set (MLOS.csv). A result should name the repository commit (451a1b16 read here) and the zip file's date or checksum.

strengths.text: Codon tokens match the unit that matters for coding sequence design, which the authors argue gives better representations.
The pretraining sequence IDs, evaluation split and downstream datasets, including a new internal dataset, are released with the code.
The authors report that CodonBERT outperforms previous mRNA prediction methods, including on a new flu vaccine dataset; this is their claim.

limitations.text: Code and weights are for academic research and non-commercial use by academic or non-profit organisations only.
Coding regions only: inputs must be codon sequences, so UTRs and non-coding RNA are outside its scope, and sequences over 512 codons were split into fragments in pretraining.
The environment is old: Python below 3.11, torch ^1.13.0 and transformers ^4.29.0, managed with Poetry.
The weights are a single zip on a company server with no version identifier, so a later change to the file would not be visible from the URL.

profile.summary: DeCodon is a generative language model for protein-coding DNA that works one codon at a time. Given an NCBI Taxonomy ID for an organism, it writes new coding sequences for that organism. It is the decoder half of the cdsFM suite, released with the encoder model EnCodon, and was pretrained on coding sequences from the NCBI Genomes database.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: introduction; Sequence Generation with DeCodon; bioRxiv abstract; config.json

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each token is one of the 64 codons or a special token. DeCodon is loaded as a causal language model: its configuration marks it as a decoder with 12 hidden layers, 16 attention heads, hidden size 1024 and rotary position embeddings. To generate, the wrapper builds a prompt from the organism's taxonomy ID in angle brackets, so the model writes a sequence conditioned on the organism, and stops at the separator token. The same wrapper also offers embedding extraction and variant scoring.

sections.body: Two DeCodon checkpoints are listed: decodon-200M, the pretrained checkpoint, and decodon-200M-euk, described only as a eukaryotic expert. Hugging Face counts 157,988,032 parameters in each, fewer than the 200M in the names. This page read decodon-200M at revision 5c5c3da1 and decodon-200M-euk at revision 89ce8d5c. A result should name the checkpoint and its revision.

profile.summary: EnCodon is a language model for protein-coding DNA that reads a coding sequence one codon at a time and returns a numerical embedding of it. The embeddings can be used as features or fine-tuned, and the package also scores codon variants by comparing model probabilities. It is part of the cdsFM suite, released with the generative model DeCodon, and was pretrained on coding sequences from the NCBI Genomes database.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: introduction; Sequence Embedding Extraction with EnCodon; bioRxiv abstract; cdsfm/encodon/_auto.py: score_variants

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each token is one of the 64 codons or one of 5 special tokens, and a start token and an end token are added around each sequence. EnCodon is loaded as a masked language model with rotary position embeddings. To embed a sequence, the wrapper runs the model, takes the hidden states of a chosen layer and averages them over the codon positions, leaving out the two special tokens. To score a variant, it compares the log probability of the alternative codon with that of the reference codon, either in the wild-type sequence or with the position masked.

sections.body: Four EnCodon checkpoints are listed, in two sizes. encodon-80M and encodon-620M are the pretrained checkpoints; encodon-80M-euk and encodon-620M-euk are described only as eukaryotic experts. The encodon-80M checkpoint has 6 layers, 8 attention heads and hidden size 1024; the encodon-620M checkpoint has 12 layers, 16 heads and hidden size 2048. The configs of the euk checkpoints were not read. This page read encodon-80M at revision 81702e23, encodon-80M-euk at 746f9f3a, encodon-620M at 87958432 and encodon-620M-euk at 3597b284. profile.summary: GPN-MSA is a DNA language model that scores human single-nucleotide variants genome-wide. It reads a window of the human genome together with the aligned sequence of other vertebrates, and scores a variant by how much less likely the alternate allele is than the reference. Its developers now mark it as deprecated in favour of GPN-Star.
profile.summary_source_locator: docs/models/gpn-msa.md, opening paragraph; model card title; cli.md, GPN section on the output score

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The published checkpoint is a 12-layer Transformer encoder (hidden size 768, 12 attention heads) trained as a masked language model. Each position is given the human nucleotide and the aligned nucleotides of the other species in the whole-genome alignment as auxiliary features, so the model predicts a masked human base from its sequence context and from what other vertebrates carry at the same site. A variant's score is the alternate-minus-reference log-likelihood ratio at its position, averaged over the forward and reverse-complement orientations. Negative values mean the alternate allele is less likely than the reference under the model.
sections.source_locator: config.json: architectures, num_hidden_layers, hidden_size, num_attention_heads, n_aux_features; cli.md: GPN and GPN-MSA sections on the output score; model card title

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One human checkpoint is published, songlab/gpn-msa-sapiens, trained on humans and 89 other vertebrates. The repository supports inference from it and no longer maintains GPN-MSA training or dataset construction. Inference needs a local alignment store whose target assembly, species count, species order and preprocessing match the checkpoint. Genome-wide hg38 scores are published as a dataset, so most uses do not need to run the model. A result should say whether it used the published scores or ran inference, and with which window size.

from gpn import register_auto_classes
from transformers import AutoModelForMaskedLM

steps.title: Score variants
steps.shell:
gpn msa vep \
  --input-path variants.parquet \
  --msa-path LOCAL_MSA_PATH \
  --window-size WINDOW_SIZE \
  --model-path songlab/gpn-msa-sapiens \
  --output-path scores.parquet
steps.explanation: Replace LOCAL_MSA_PATH with the path to the alignment store and WINDOW_SIZE with an even number. The documentation read does not give the window size for this checkpoint. The reference allele must match the alignment at each position or inference stops.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RNA-MSM follows the protein MSA Transformer design: an embedding module with two learned position embeddings, one for the rows (sequences in the MSA) and one for the columns (positions), then 10 transformer blocks with 12 attention heads each and a 768-dimensional embedding. The authors cut the block count from 12 to 10 because of GPU memory. It was trained with the BERT masked language modelling objective, masking 20% of MSA tokens. The 120 attention maps (10 blocks by 12 heads) and the embedding of the query sequence are the outputs; separate downstream networks in the repository turn them into secondary structure and solvent accessibility predictions.
sections.source_locator: paper: Materials and methods; Figure 1 legend; README.md: Inference; RNA_MSM_Inference.py

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One pretrained checkpoint is released on Google Drive (RNA_MSM_pretrained.ckpt by the script's default path). The repository also carries trained downstream models for secondary structure and solvent accessibility, and the downstream datasets with their MSAs were released in July 2024. Results depend strongly on the MSA, so a result should name the checkpoint, the repository commit, and the homology search tool and settings used to build the MSA.

name: RNABERT
description: RNA language model pre-trained on small non-coding RNA.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Described in You et al. 2026, Table 1.

profile.summary: RNABERT is a small RNA language model from Keio University that turns each base of a non-coding RNA sequence into a numerical vector (an embedding) that reflects its sequence context and secondary structure. It reads RNA sequences in FASTA format and outputs per-base embeddings, which the authors use to align RNAs by structure and to cluster them into RNA families.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Introduction; README.md: Data processing, Earn embeddings

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each base gets a 120-dimensional token embedding plus a position embedding, and the sum passes through six Transformer layers. The output is a context-sensitive embedding for every base. Training alternates two tasks. In masked language modelling (MLM), some bases are hidden and predicted from the rest. In structural alignment learning (SAL), pairs of sequences from Rfam seed alignments are aligned using their embeddings, so that bases aligned in the reference alignment get similar embeddings. A structural alignment of two RNAs is then computed from the embeddings with the Needleman-Wunsch algorithm.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Figure 2 caption; Introduction; Discussion

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One pre-trained model file is offered, through a Google Drive link in the README, with no version number. The README says this model was trained on the full Rfam 14.3 dataset (about 400 nucleotides), while the paper describes MLM pre-training on 76 237 human small ncRNAs from RNAcentral and SAL training on Rfam alignments (TrainSet-A or TrainSet-B). Which of the paper's settings the download matches is not stated. A result should cite the repository commit and say that the Google Drive model was used.

name: RNAErnie
description: RNA language model with motif-aware pre-training.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Described in You et al. 2026, Table 1.

profile.summary: RNAErnie is an RNA language model that turns an RNA sequence into embeddings for downstream prediction. During pretraining it uses known RNA motifs as prior knowledge and masks them at random, alongside the usual masked language modelling. Its developers fine-tune it for RNA sequence classification, RNA-RNA interaction prediction and RNA secondary structure prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening paragraphs

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The original RNAErnie is built on the ERNIE model in PaddlePaddle and pretrained with masked language modelling on RNAcentral sequences of up to 512 nucleotides. The released checkpoint combines the BERT, ERNIE and motif masking strategies. Downstream, the developers offer an optional two-stage, type-guided fine-tuning. For RNA secondary structure prediction the repository uses a folding module compiled from mxfold2. The authors' later PyTorch checkpoint is a BERT masked language model with 12 layers, hidden size 768, 12 attention heads and an 11-token vocabulary.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Pre-training, Extract RNA Sequence Embeddings, Downstream Tasks; config.json of the PyTorch checkpoint

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There are two lines of checkpoints. The original PaddlePaddle model from the paper, with masking-strategy variants and task-specific fine-tuned weights, is distributed through Google Drive folders linked from the README; an ad-hoc variant pretrained with an extra classification loss and a 1-epoch checkpoint are also linked. In June 2024 the developers trained a separate PyTorch model from scratch with a maximum length of 2048 on a newer RNAcentral release of about 31 million sequences, and published it on Hugging Face (now LLM-EDA/RNAErnie); its tokenisation differs slightly from the original. A result should say which of these checkpoints was used.

run_guide.summary: Set up the original PaddlePaddle RNAErnie environment and extract embeddings for three example RNA sequences with the pretrained checkpoint.
prerequisites: Conda, and a GPU: the environment installs paddlepaddle-gpu 2.3.2 and the example sets the device to gpu.

The pretrained checkpoint files (.pdparams and .json) downloaded by hand from the Google Drive folder linked in the README and placed in ./output/BERT,ERNIE,MOTIF,PROMPT so that output/BERT,ERNIE,MOTIF,PROMPT/checkpoint_final/ exists. The README does not state the folder layout inside the download.
The environment file pins Linux conda builds and a Tsinghua mirror channel, so it may not resolve on other platforms.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/CatIIIIIIII/RNAErnie.git
cd ./RNAErnie
git checkout --detach b5e4c1cfdc6f53101111823abaddcab00c43b0d3
steps.explanation: Clones the repository as in the README. The checkout line is added to pin the commit read for this page.

steps.shell:
conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate RNAErnie
steps.explanation: Creates the conda environment named RNAErnie with Python 3.8 and PaddlePaddle.

steps.title: Extract embeddings
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import paddle
from rna_ernie import BatchConverter
from paddlenlp.transformers import ErnieModel

# ========== Set device
paddle.set_device("gpu")

# ========== Prepare Data
data = [
    ("RNA1", "GGGUGCGAUCAUACCAGCACUAAUGCCCUCCUGGGAAGUCCUCGUGUUGCACCCCU"),
    ("RNA2", "GGGUGUCGCUCAGUUGGUAGAGUGCUUGCCUGGCAUGCAAGAAACCUUGGUUCAAUCCCCAGCACUGCA"),
    ("RNA3", "CGAUUCNCGUUCCC--CCGCCUCCA"),
]

# ========== Batch Converter
batch_converter = BatchConverter(k_mer=1,
                                  vocab_path="./data/vocab/vocab_1MER.txt",
                                  batch_size=256,
                                  max_seq_len=512)

# ========== RNAErnie Model
rna_ernie = ErnieModel.from_pretrained("output/BERT,ERNIE,MOTIF,PROMPT/checkpoint_final/")
rna_ernie.eval()

# call batch_converter to convert sequences to batch inputs
for names, _, inputs_ids in batch_converter(data):
    with paddle.no_grad():
        # extract whole sequence embeddings
        embeddings = rna_ernie(inputs_ids)[0].detach()
        # extract [CLS] token embedding
        embeddings_cls = embeddings[:, 0, :]
        print(names, embeddings.shape, embeddings_cls.shape)
PY

name: SpTransformer
description: Task-specific transformer for tissue-specific splice site prediction.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Described in You et al. 2026, Introduction.

profile.summary: SpliceTransformer (SpTransformer) predicts RNA splicing from genomic sequence alone. For each position in a pre-mRNA sequence it gives the probability of being a splice donor, a splice acceptor or neither, and how much the site is used in each of 15 human tissues. Comparing predictions for reference and variant sequence lets it score how a genetic variant changes splicing in each tissue.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, Tissue-specific prediction of splicing; Fig. 1 caption. README: title paragraph

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SpTransformer has two main modules. An encoder of stacked convolutional residual blocks (ResBlocks) reads one-hot encoded sequence; the paper uses two such encoders with identical structure. Their output feeds a Sinkhorn Transformer, an attention variant built for long sequences, with 256 channels, 8 attention heads (two of them local) per layer and eight layers, followed by a multi-layer perceptron. For a 9000 nt input it predicts the central 1000 nt, using 4000 nt of context on each side. The output is an N x 3 matrix for splice site class and an N x 15 matrix for tissue usage. Training ran in two stages: first the two encoders were trained separately, one on GTEx data and one on an extra mammalian dataset, with 12 epochs per stage.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, SpTransformer model structure; Data representation; Model training

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository describes one trained model. Its weights are too large for GitHub; Git-LFS access was disabled in November 2024, and the weights are now a single Google Drive download placed in model/weights. The download has no version label, so a result can only name the repository commit (this page read b67a51da) and the date the weights were fetched. The authors note that outputs can differ slightly between GPU types for individual variants. The variant annotation script uses a 95% threshold for tissue specificity unless raw scores are requested, so a result should say which output mode was used.

name: UTR-LM
description: Language model pre-trained on 5' untranslated region sequence.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Described in You et al. 2026, Table 1.

profile.summary: UTR-LM is a language model for the 5' untranslated region (5' UTR) of mRNA, the stretch before the coding sequence that strongly affects how well an mRNA is translated. It reads a 5' UTR sequence and, after fine-tuning, predicts mean ribosome loading, translation efficiency or mRNA expression level. Pretraining combines masked language modelling with labels computed from the sequence, such as secondary structure and minimum free energy.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md opening paragraph; bioRxiv abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: UTR-LM is built on a modified copy of the ESM-2 transformer code, shipped in the repository. The reported settings are 6 transformer layers, 16 attention heads and an embedding size of 128. Pretraining uses masked language modelling (MLM) and, in the recommended variants, also predicts the minimum free energy (MFE) and/or the secondary structure of the sequence. For downstream tasks the developers fine-tune the whole model and feed the [CLS]-token embedding to a predictor trained with Huber loss.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Install step 3; General Parameters; UTR-LM pretraining process

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository holds 16 pretrained checkpoint files under Model/Pretrained, named by their pretraining variant (ESM2, ESM2SI, ESM2SS, ESM2SISS, ESM2DSD) and data split, plus 182 files under Model/Downstream for the MRL, TE and EL tasks. The README's own example pretraining command passes --heads 6 --embed_dim 16, which disagrees with the 16 heads and embedding size 128 listed under General Parameters and in the checkpoint file names. A result should name the exact checkpoint file and the repository commit. A runnable copy is also published as a CodeOcean capsule.

profile.summary: DeepAffinity predicts compound-protein affinity from a compound SMILES string and a structure property-annotated protein sequence (SPS), using pretrained recurrent seq2seq encoders followed by convolutional layers.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GRU seq2seq auto-encoders are first trained without labels on compound SMILES and protein SPS strings. In the unified RNN-CNN model, a 1D convolution and max-pooling layer is added after each encoder, the two outputs are concatenated and passed through two fully connected layers, and the whole pipeline is trained end to end with the pretrained encoders as initialisation. A separate RNN-CNN baseline keeps the encoders fixed.

sections.title: Protein representation
sections.body: In the original paper, SPS strings group residues into secondary structure elements using secondary structure and solvent accessibility predicted from sequence by SSpro/ACCpro.

sections.title: Variants
sections.body: The paper also describes separate, marginalized and joint attention mechanisms trained jointly with the encoders and CNN, and a unified RNN/GCNN-CNN variant that replaces the compound RNN with a graph CNN.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SMILES strings and protein sequences are label-encoded characters. Each passes through its own block of three 1D convolutional layers, where the second and third layers have two and three times the filters of the first, followed by max-pooling. The two pooled vectors are concatenated and fed into fully connected layers of 1,024, 1,024 and 512 units, with dropout after the first two, and a regression output trained with mean squared error.

profile.summary: hEvo is a family of DNA language models from MulinLab trained on haplotype sequences from human populations, so that the models see real human genetic variation rather than one reference genome. A model reads a DNA sequence of up to 1,024 nucleotides and returns one vector per nucleotide, plus masked-base predictions that can score a single-nucleotide variant as a log-likelihood ratio of the alternative against the reference allele. The authors use it for variant-effect scoring, regulatory annotation and population-genetic analysis.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: Overview, Models; hEVO-base-o card: Model overview, Intended use

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: hEvo is a bidirectional BERT-style masked language model with one token per nucleotide. Training has two stages. In Stage I the model learns representations by span masking on deduplicated haplotype windows drawn from population haplotypes. In Stage II the nucleotide prediction head is calibrated on contexts centred on variants. To score a single-nucleotide variant, the variant position is masked once and the log probability of the alternative allele minus that of the reference allele is taken from the same masked context; a positive value means the model prefers the alternative allele.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Two stages of learning, Models; hEVO-base-o card: Model overview, Single-nucleotide variant scoring

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The README lists primary models hEvo-base and hEvo-large, and public-data variants hEvo-open-base and hEvo-open-large, which are published on Hugging Face as hEVO-base-o (87.1M parameters, 12 layers, hidden size 768) and hEVO-large-o (319.5M parameters, 16 layers, hidden size 1,280). Only the two -o checkpoints are linked for download, and both are gated. The -o models were pretrained separately on public 1000 Genomes Project and HGDP data. The README says hEVO-base-o matches the hEvo-open-base weights by file hash, and that hEVO-large-o has identical tensors to the hEvo-open-large checkpoint after conversion. The model cards pin a code and weights revision in their examples (fa613904 for base, 09541834 for large) and keep the card itself on main. A result should name the checkpoint and that revision.

steps.title: Load the model and embed a sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'EOF'
import torch
from transformers import AutoConfig, AutoModelForMaskedLM, AutoTokenizer

REPO = "MulinLab/hEVO-base-o"
# Freeze the checkpoint and its custom code for reproducible inference.
REVISION = "fa6139047c21d92b58bd8eda49ea2f89a884e33c"
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

load_options = dict(revision=REVISION, token=True, trust_remote_code=True)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(REPO, **load_options)
config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(
    REPO,
    use_frequency_embedding=False,
    use_flash_attention=False,
    **load_options,
)
assert config.use_frequency_embedding is False
model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained(
    REPO,
    config=config,
    attn_implementation="eager",
    dtype=torch.float32,
    **load_options,
).to(device).eval()

def encode_dna(sequence):
    sequence = sequence.strip().upper()
    if not 0 < len(sequence) <= config.max_position_embeddings:
        raise ValueError("Provide a sequence of 1 to 1,024 nucleotides.")
    if set(sequence) - set("ACGTN"):
        raise ValueError("DNA must contain only A, C, G, T or N.")
    encoded = tokenizer(sequence, return_tensors="pt", truncation=False)
    # This custom tokenizer returns 1D tensors for a single sequence.
    encoded = {
        key: value.unsqueeze(0) if value.ndim == 1 else value
        for key, value in encoded.items()
    }
    if "attention_mask" not in encoded:
        encoded["attention_mask"] = torch.ones_like(encoded["input_ids"])
    return {key: value.to(device) for key, value in encoded.items()}

sequence = "ACGTTGCATGTCGCATGATGCATGAGAGCT"
inputs = encode_dna(sequence)

with torch.inference_mode():
    outputs = model(**inputs, output_hidden_states=True, return_dict=True)
    token_embeddings = outputs.hidden_states[-1]  # [batch, length, hidden_size]

    # Optional: summarize the last-layer nucleotide embeddings by mean pooling.
    keep = inputs["attention_mask"].unsqueeze(-1).to(token_embeddings.dtype)
    sequence_embedding = (token_embeddings * keep).sum(dim=1) / keep.sum(
        dim=1
    ).clamp_min(1)

print("Last-layer token embeddings:", tuple(token_embeddings.shape))
print("Mean-pooled sequence embedding:", tuple(sequence_embedding.shape))
EOF

sections.body: hEVO-base-o is a bidirectional BERT-style masked language model with 12 transformer layers and hidden size 768, and one token per nucleotide with no boundary tokens. The family README describes two training stages: span-masked representation learning on deduplicated haplotype windows, then calibration of the nucleotide prediction head on variant-centred contexts. To score a single-nucleotide variant, the variant site is masked once and the alternative-allele logit minus the reference-allele logit at that site gives the log-likelihood ratio. The weight file also holds tensors for an optional frequency branch, which is off by default and not built when loading.

steps.title: Load the model and embed a sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'EOF'
import torch
from transformers import AutoConfig, AutoModelForMaskedLM, AutoTokenizer

REPO = "MulinLab/hEVO-base-o"
# Freeze the checkpoint and its custom code for reproducible inference.
REVISION = "fa6139047c21d92b58bd8eda49ea2f89a884e33c"
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

load_options = dict(revision=REVISION, token=True, trust_remote_code=True)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(REPO, **load_options)
config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(
    REPO,
    use_frequency_embedding=False,
    use_flash_attention=False,
    **load_options,
)
assert config.use_frequency_embedding is False
model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained(
    REPO,
    config=config,
    attn_implementation="eager",
    dtype=torch.float32,
    **load_options,
).to(device).eval()

def encode_dna(sequence):
    sequence = sequence.strip().upper()
    if not 0 < len(sequence) <= config.max_position_embeddings:
        raise ValueError("Provide a sequence of 1 to 1,024 nucleotides.")
    if set(sequence) - set("ACGTN"):
        raise ValueError("DNA must contain only A, C, G, T or N.")
    encoded = tokenizer(sequence, return_tensors="pt", truncation=False)
    # This custom tokenizer returns 1D tensors for a single sequence.
    encoded = {
        key: value.unsqueeze(0) if value.ndim == 1 else value
        for key, value in encoded.items()
    }
    if "attention_mask" not in encoded:
        encoded["attention_mask"] = torch.ones_like(encoded["input_ids"])
    return {key: value.to(device) for key, value in encoded.items()}

sequence = "ACGTTGCATGTCGCATGATGCATGAGAGCT"
inputs = encode_dna(sequence)

with torch.inference_mode():
    outputs = model(**inputs, output_hidden_states=True, return_dict=True)
    token_embeddings = outputs.hidden_states[-1]  # [batch, length, hidden_size]

    # Optional: summarize the last-layer nucleotide embeddings by mean pooling.
    keep = inputs["attention_mask"].unsqueeze(-1).to(token_embeddings.dtype)
    sequence_embedding = (token_embeddings * keep).sum(dim=1) / keep.sum(
        dim=1
    ).clamp_min(1)

print("Last-layer token embeddings:", tuple(token_embeddings.shape))
print("Mean-pooled sequence embedding:", tuple(sequence_embedding.shape))
EOF

profile.summary: LncRFM is an RNA foundation model built for long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), whose function depends on both short sequence motifs and base pairing that can span thousands of nucleotides. It reads an RNA sequence and is pretrained to predict masked nucleotides, with masking guided by secondary structure; its encoder outputs can then be fine-tuned with a small task head for tasks such as lncRNA localisation, disease association or splice-site prediction. The authors also release the LncCorpus pretraining corpus and the LncBench benchmark.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LncRFM is a hybrid bidirectional state-space encoder. Its state-space kernels build on Mamba, and its bidirectional backbone follows the Hydra and HydraRNA design. The model code requires a motif stem, a motif gate and a pair-aware bidirectional mixer. The released configuration has 12 layers of width 768, motif convolution kernels of sizes 3 and 7, and attention layers with 12 heads at positions 5 and 11. It is pretrained by masked language modelling, using a structure-aware masking collator adapted from RNAErnie2 and training data that records each base's pairing partner. The pretraining launcher uses FP32, sequences of 200 to 2,048 nucleotides and 300,000 steps.

steps.title: Predict a masked nucleotide
steps.shell:
python - <<'EOF'
from pathlib import Path
import json
import torch
from lncrfm import get_lncrfm, get_tokenizer

checkpoint = Path("checkpoints/lncrfm_pretrained")
options = json.loads((checkpoint / "model_config.json").read_text())["factory_kwargs"]
tokenizer = get_tokenizer(
    tokenizer_file=str(checkpoint / "tokenizer.json"),
    max_length=options["max_length"],
)
model = get_lncrfm(
    **options,
    tokenizer=tokenizer,
    from_pretrained=str(checkpoint),
    dtype=torch.float32,
    device="cuda",
).eval()

inputs = tokenizer("[CLS] A U G [MASK] C [SEP]", return_tensors="pt").to("cuda")
with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model(**inputs)
print(outputs.logits.argmax(dim=-1))
EOF
steps.explanation: The README's loading and inference example, wrapped in a shell heredoc. It reads the model settings from the checkpoint and runs on CUDA.

outputs: test_model.py prints a PASS line for each check it runs, for example that the architecture and the checkpoint tensors match. The inference example prints the index of the most likely token at each input position, including the masked one.

profile.summary: LIMBER is an RNA language model for non-coding RNA. It reads an RNA sequence one nucleotide at a time and returns per-nucleotide embeddings and masked-token predictions, which the authors use for secondary-structure prediction, RNA family classification and mutational fitness scoring.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md at commit 72a328a: Overview and Quick start; preprint abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LIMBER stacks two kinds of layer in a repeating Transformer, Transformer, Mamba pattern. The Transformer layers use bidirectional self-attention, which relates any two positions directly; the authors link this to the long-range coupling that base pairing leaves in a sequence. The Mamba layers are selective state-space layers that process the sequence in order. The model is pretrained by masked language modelling: 15% of nucleotide positions are selected, and of those 80% are replaced by a mask token, 10% by a random nucleotide and 10% left unchanged. Tokenisation is one token per nucleotide over a 10-token vocabulary; T is mapped to U and any other symbol to N.
sections.source_locator: README.md at commit 72a328a: Overview; Model zoo; Tokenization; Pretraining

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Five LIMBER sizes are released, from 10.2M to 664.3M parameters, with size-matched pure-Transformer and pure-Mamba models trained on the same data. The README counts 25 checkpoints in one Hugging Face repository, one subfolder per model, including data-fraction, training-epoch and shape ablations. A result should name the subfolder it used: LIMBER-macro, LIMBER-meso and LIMBER-nano differ in depth and width, not only in size. The Hugging Face repository was at revision d2d6ae6 when read on 2026-11-26.
sections.source_locator: README.md at commit 72a328a: Model zoo; Hugging Face file listing at revision d2d6ae6

sections.title: What the authors report
sections.body: The authors fine-tuned LIMBER and each baseline themselves under one protocol. They report a median flexible F1 of 0.895 on bpRNA TS0 and 0.816 on Rivas TestSetB for LIMBER-macro, and 99.2% accuracy on the 13-class nRC benchmark. On IRES identification and 5'UTR mean ribosome load, RiNALMo-giga scores higher than LIMBER-macro on most metrics in the same tables. These are author-reported figures and are not yet recorded as results in this database.

steps.title: Get embeddings from Python
steps.shell:

model, _ = load_hybrid()

profile.summary: BMRetriever-7B is a biomedical text embedding model for dense retrieval. It turns a query (with a one-sentence task instruction) or a passage into a 4096-dimensional vector, and relevance is scored as the dot product between query and passage vectors. It is the largest of four BMRetriever models and is built on the BioMistral 7B language model, further trained on biomedical corpora and instruction data.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; README: Model Specifications, Model Usage; model card: Usage

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: BMRetriever starts from a pretrained language model (BioMistral for the 7B model), runs unsupervised pre-training on large biomedical corpora, then instruction fine-tuning on labelled datasets and synthetic pairs. At inference, each query is prefixed with a one-sentence task instruction, each passage with 'Represent this passage', and an end-of-sequence token is appended. The embedding is the final hidden state at the last token (last-token pooling). The 7B model is a 32-layer Mistral architecture with hidden size 4096.

The instruction fine-tuning data, about 1.4M pairs, is released as BMRetriever/biomed_retrieval_dataset, and eval.py and prompt.py reproduce the BEIR experiments. run_guide.summary: Load BMRetriever-7B from Hugging Face, embed two example queries and two passages, and print their dot-product similarity scores.
prerequisites: Python with PyTorch and Hugging Face transformers installed; the sources give no install command. The config was saved with transformers 4.37.2.
A CUDA GPU: the example moves inputs to 'cuda'. Memory needs are not stated; the weights are float32 with 7,110,660,096 parameters.
Weights and code are MIT licensed; the weights are not gated.

steps.title: Embed and score example texts
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("BMRetriever/BMRetriever-7B") 
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("BMRetriever/BMRetriever-7B") 

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

from torch import Tensor
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel


def last_token_pool(last_hidden_states: Tensor,
                 attention_mask: Tensor) -> Tensor:
    last_hidden = last_hidden_states.masked_fill(~attention_mask[..., None].bool(), 0.0)
    left_padding = (attention_mask[:, -1].sum() == attention_mask.shape[0])
    if left_padding:
        embedding = last_hidden[:, -1]
    else:
        sequence_lengths = attention_mask.sum(dim=1) - 1
        batch_size = last_hidden.shape[0]
        embedding = last_hidden[torch.arange(batch_size, device=last_hidden.device), sequence_lengths]
    return embedding

def get_detailed_instruct_query(task_description: str, query: str) -> str:
    return f'{task_description}\nQuery: {query}'

def get_detailed_instruct_passage(passage: str) -> str:
    return f'Represent this passage\npassage: {passage}'

# Each query must come with a one-sentence instruction that describes the task
task = 'Given a scientific claim, retrieve documents that support or refute the claim'
queries = [
    get_detailed_instruct_query(task, 'Cis-acting lncRNAs control the expression of genes that are positioned in the vicinity of their transcription sites.'),
    get_detailed_instruct_query(task, 'Forkhead 0 (fox0) transcription factors are involved in apoptosis.')
]

# No need to add instruction for retrieval documents
documents = [
    get_detailed_instruct_passage("Gene regulation by the act of long non-coding RNA transcription Long non-protein-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are proposed to be the largest transcript class in the mouse and human transcriptomes. Two important questions are whether all lncRNAs are functional and how they could exert a function. Several lncRNAs have been shown to function through their product, but this is not the only possible mode of action. In this review we focus on a role for the process of lncRNA transcription, independent of the lncRNA product, in regulating protein-coding-gene activity in cis. We discuss examples where lncRNA transcription leads to gene silencing or activation, and describe strategies to determine if the lncRNA product or its transcription causes the regulatory effect."),
    get_detailed_instruct_passage("Noncoding transcription at enhancers: general principles and functional models. Mammalian genomes are extensively transcribed outside the borders of protein-coding genes. Genome-wide studies recently demonstrated that cis-regulatory genomic elements implicated in transcriptional control, such as enhancers and locus-control regions, represent major sites of extragenic noncoding transcription. Enhancer-templated transcripts provide a quantitatively small contribution to the total amount of cellular nonribosomal RNA; nevertheless, the possibility that enhancer transcription and the resulting enhancer RNAs may, in some cases, have functional roles, rather than represent mere transcriptional noise at accessible genomic regions, is supported by an increasing amount of experimental data. In this article we review the current knowledge on enhancer transcription and its functional implications.")
]
input_texts = queries + documents

max_length = 512

# Tokenize the input texts
batch_dict = tokenizer(input_texts, max_length=max_length-1, padding=True, truncation=True, return_tensors='pt')

# Important! Adding EOS token at the end
batch_dict['input_ids'] = [input_ids + [tokenizer.eos_token_id] for input_ids in batch_dict['input_ids']]
batch_dict = tokenizer.pad(batch_dict, padding=True, return_attention_mask=True, return_tensors='pt').to("cuda")

model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model(**batch_dict)
    embeddings = last_token_pool(outputs.last_hidden_state, batch_dict['attention_mask'])

scores = (embeddings[:2] @ embeddings[2:].T)
print(scores.tolist())
PY

profile.summary: BulkFormer is a family of foundation models for human bulk RNA-seq. A model takes one expression profile per sample, covering about twenty thousand protein-coding genes, and returns either a single vector that represents the whole sample or a vector per gene plus recovered expression values. Those vectors are then used as frozen features for downstream prediction, for example disease classification, prognosis or drug response.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: header and Choose a model; docs/original-paper.md: Abstract; docs/architecture.md; docs/models/atlas.md

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The two current models work differently. Atlas gives each gene a token that combines a learned identity embedding with a linear projection of log2(TPM + 1), then passes a CLS token and up to 4,096 selected gene tokens through 16 bidirectional transformer blocks of width 1,024 with 16 heads and SwiGLU feed-forward layers; the sample feature is the 1,024-dimensional CLS output taken before the projection head. Latest encodes all 19,973 gene positions at once: gene identity, a sinusoidal encoding of expression and a global expression MLP (19,973 to 2,560 to 768) are normalised separately and summed with fixed 1:1:1 coefficients, then a residual weighted graph convolution of hidden width 256 feeds a 12-layer Performer of width 768. A small network reads how much of the input is missing and applies a bounded gain and offset to the expression head.
sections.source_locator: docs/architecture.md; configs/atlas_model.json; configs/latest_model.json

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three generations sit in one repository. The publication family has five sizes: 37M, 50M, 93M, 127M and 147M parameters, with the authors recommending 147M where resources allow. The 2026-11-04 release added BulkFormer-Atlas (242.37M) and BulkFormer-Latest (154.55M), and on 2026-11-06 Latest moved to its final epoch-20 checkpoint. Each new model carries an immutable checkpoint ID: atlas-infonce-epoch10-update320000 and latest-20261106-epoch20-update148300. The repository is explicit that published PRIMO scores were produced by earlier checkpoints: Atlas appears as BulkFormer-variant, and the epoch-19 Latest as BulkFormer-V3Plus, whose scores do not evaluate the current download. A result should name the model, the checkpoint ID and the pooling protocol.

profile.summary: BulkRNABert is a transformer language model for bulk RNA-seq data. It takes the expression levels of a fixed set of genes from one sample and returns embeddings of that sample. The embeddings are used to build downstream models for cancer-type classification and survival-time prediction.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: BulkRNABert is an encoder-only transformer. Each gene in the input is one token, and its expression value is binned and embedded together with a gene embedding. During pretraining, expression values are masked at random and the model learns to reconstruct them from the other genes, as in BERT. The released configuration has 4 transformer layers, an embedding size of 256, 8 attention heads, 64 expression bins and 19,062 genes. For a downstream task the authors either probe the learned embeddings or use parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

sections.body: The repository ships three pretrained checkpoints in JAX: bulk_rna_bert_tcga (pretrained on TCGA), bulk_rna_bert_gtex_encode (GTEx and ENCODE) and bulk_rna_bert_gtex_encode_tcga (a mix of all three). It also ships a classification model for five TCGA cohorts used in an example notebook. The Hugging Face repository InstaDeepAI/BulkRNABert holds a PyTorch version for the transformers library, described as pretrained on TCGA, plus the JAX parameters. A result should name the checkpoint, the framework and the commit or Hugging Face revision; this page read the repository at commit bfdc2ab8 and the Hugging Face card at revision 4ee84d56.

sections.title: Input preparation
sections.body: The model expects expression values for a fixed list of genes, given in common_gene_id.txt, in a fixed order. The repository includes a script that turns raw RNA-seq files downloaded from the GDC portal into this format, using the unstranded TPM column in its example. The Hugging Face example applies log10(1 + x) to the expression values before tokenising and checks that the number of columns equals the model's gene count.

strengths.text: Weights for three pretraining datasets are released, so a user can compare a TCGA-only model with one trained on non-cancer tissue (GTEx and ENCODE) or a mix.
Code and weights are under Apache-2.0, and the Hugging Face weights are not gated.
The repository includes sample TCGA data, the gene list and a preprocessing script for raw GDC files, so the input format can be reproduced.

The authors report that it improves on previous methods for pan-cancer classification and survival analysis on TCGA, and that it transfers to unseen cohorts in survival analysis. This is the authors' own claim.

limitations.text: The input is a fixed list of 19,062 genes in a fixed order. Data from another gene annotation or platform must be mapped onto this list first.
The model gives embeddings, not predictions. Classification or survival needs a downstream model; only a five-cohort classifier and a pan-cancer survival checkpoint are shipped.
