run_guide.summary: Install the repository package at a pinned commit and compute BulkRNABert embeddings for the bundled TCGA sample with the bulk_rna_bert_tcga checkpoint.
prerequisites: Python 3.10 or later, as setup.py requires.
The package pins jax==0.4.19, jaxlib==0.4.19 and dm-haiku==0.0.10. GPU type and memory are not stated in the sources read.
Code and weights are Apache-2.0; the sample TCGA data stay under their source's terms.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/instadeepai/multiomics-open-research.git
cd multiomics-open-research
git checkout --detach bfdc2ab8d7692aa6fba0f7879b4886a73ec6c700
steps.explanation: The README says to clone the repository but gives no command; the clone, cd and checkout lines are added to get the commit this page was written from. The JAX checkpoints are stored in the repository's checkpoints/ folder.

steps.title: Install the package
steps.shell: pip install -e .
steps.explanation: Installs the multiomics_open_research package and its pinned dependencies.

steps.title: Compute embeddings for the sample data
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import haiku as hk
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import pandas as pd

from multiomics_open_research.bulk_rna_bert.pretrained import get_bulkrnabert_pretrained_model
from multiomics_open_research.common.preprocess import preprocess_omic

# Get pretrained model
parameters, forward_fn, tokenizer, config = get_bulkrnabert_pretrained_model(
    model_name="bulk_rna_bert_tcga",
    embeddings_layers_to_save=(4,),
    checkpoint_directory="checkpoints/",
)
forward_fn = hk.transform(forward_fn)

# Get bulk RNASeq data and tokenize it
gene_expression_df = pd.read_csv("data/bulkrnabert/tcga_sample.csv")
gene_expression_array = preprocess_omic(gene_expression_df, config)
gene_expression_ids = tokenizer.batch_tokenize(gene_expression_array)
gene_expression_ids = jnp.asarray(gene_expression_ids, dtype=jnp.int32)

# Inference
random_key = jax.random.PRNGKey(0)
outs = forward_fn.apply(parameters, random_key, gene_expression_ids)

# Get mean embeddings from layer 4
gene_expression_mean_embeddings = outs["embeddings_4"].mean(axis=1)
PY
steps.explanation: The README inference snippet, wrapped in a shell heredoc and run from the repository root. Replace bulk_rna_bert_tcga with bulk_rna_bert_gtex_encode or bulk_rna_bert_gtex_encode_tcga to use the other checkpoints.

outputs: An array of mean layer-4 embeddings, one row per sample in tcga_sample.csv, held in memory. The snippet prints nothing and writes no file.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
The guide stops at embeddings. Classification or survival prediction needs a downstream model, as in the repository's example notebook.
Own data must first be converted to the model's gene list, for example with scripts/preprocess_tcga_rna_seq.py for GDC files.

profile.summary: Ladon is a foundation model for bulk RNA sequencing of tumours, built by the company Blank Bio. It learns from millions of RNA-seq profiles by reconstructing masked parts of isoform-level expression, and its embeddings are then used to predict patient survival, recurrence and response to treatment. The developers present it as a way to make RNA-based predictions that still hold in clinical trials and cohorts the model was not fitted on.
profile.summary_source_locator: Report page 1 (abstract); page 2, Introducing Ladon

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Ladon is a transformer encoder-decoder of 3 billion parameters. It is pretrained self-supervised, by masked token reconstruction on isoform-level expression profiles, so it can learn from samples without outcome labels. For clinical use the developers then mid-train it with supervision to predict patient and tumour characteristics such as disease stage, age, tumour grade and genomic alterations, together with clinical outcomes. They then discard the prediction heads, freeze the encoder and fit simple outcome models, such as linear Cox survival models, on its embeddings. The report does not describe the layers, tokenisation or training corpus in more detail.
sections.source_locator: Report page 2, Introducing Ladon; page 11, Methods: Ladon representations; page 6; page 28, Methods

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The report describes one model family and several adaptations of it (pretrained encoder, supervised mid-training with survival or response labels), and shows models of several sizes and training steps in its scaling figures, but names no released checkpoint. No weights, code or data release is listed with the report. On 2026-11-26 the GitHub organisation blankbio had 0 public repositories and the Hugging Face organisation BlankBio had 0 models and 0 datasets. Results from Ladon cannot be reproduced independently from public material.
sections.source_locator: Report pages 11, 41 to 42 (Figures 20 and 21, Methods: Reconstruction loss); GitHub org API; Hugging Face org overview

sections.title: Evaluation in the report
sections.body: Every result is reported on a setting not used for fitting: a held-out trial, another cohort or another platform. Survival models fitted on TCGA were applied unchanged to CPTAC and the reverse; the developers report Ladon ahead of differential gene expression signatures, BulkRNABERT and BulkFormer, and that adding Ladon to clinical covariates improved survival prediction in all 12 target cohorts. They also report better response prediction for immunotherapy than PD-L1 expression, recovery of isoform usage from gene-level counts (median Pearson r of 0.81 across 3,000 genes in held-out tumours), and cell-composition inference from single-cell references. All of these are the developers' own results in an unreviewed report.

name: Akita
description: Akita contact-map model.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: Akita predicts how a stretch of DNA folds in three dimensions. It takes just over one megabase of sequence, one-hot encoded, and returns a predicted contact map for that window, as log observed over expected values, for each of five cell types it was trained on. It is used for in silico work: saturation mutagenesis, interpreting eQTLs, predicting the effect of structural variants and comparing species.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract (Europe PMC record); params.json: model; targets.txt; explore_model.ipynb

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Akita is a convolutional network in two halves. A 1D trunk reads the one-hot sequence: a convolution block, then a tower of ten convolution and pooling blocks, then eight dilated residual blocks, which brings 1,048,576 bases down to 2,048 bp bins. A 2D head turns the 1D representation into a pairwise map (one_to_two with a mean operation), concatenates a distance encoding, symmetrises it, applies six dilated 2D residual blocks, crops the edges and reads off the upper triangle with a diagonal offset of 2. The final layer has five linear units, one per training dataset. Training used mean squared error with SGD, batch size 2, and reverse-complement and shift augmentation. The published model has 751,653 parameters, of which 746,149 are trainable.
sections.source_locator: params.json: model trunk and head_hic, train; keras_print.txt; explore_model.ipynb

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There are two generations. The published model is a single TensorFlow checkpoint, model_best.h5, trained on human Hi-C and micro-C mapped to hg38 at 2048 bp resolution, with params.json as its configuration. In 2021 the authors retrained Akita on human and mouse data together after a further hyperparameter search, splitting the genome into eight folds and training one model per held-out fold; those data and models sit in Google Cloud Storage under gs://basenji_hic/3-2021, with model file suffix 0 for human and 1 for mouse. A result should say which generation and, for the 2021 set, which fold and species. This page read the repository at commit 06ce5d38.

strengths.text: Small model, about 750 thousand parameters, and the authors say that once trained it gives rapid in silico predictions.
One forward pass gives maps for five cell types at once, so cell-type differences can be read from the same prediction.

Code, model configuration, weights download, training data and a notebook that predicts from an arbitrary sequence are all published under Apache-2.0, and the repository also holds the training scripts.

limitations.text: The window is fixed at 2^20 bases and the output is binned to 2048 bp, so interactions beyond about one megabase are out of reach and the notebook refuses sequences of any other length.

steps.title: Load the model and predict from a sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import json, os, subprocess
os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = '-1' ### run on CPU

import pysam
from basenji import dna_io, seqnn

with open('params.json') as params_open:

seqnn_model = seqnn.SeqNN(params_model)
seqnn_model.restore('model_best.h5')
print('successfully loaded')

os.makedirs('./data', exist_ok=True)
if not os.path.isfile('./data/hg38.ml.fa'):
    print('downloading hg38.ml.fa')
    subprocess.call('curl -o ./data/hg38.ml.fa.gz https://storage.googleapis.com/basenji_barnyard2/hg38.ml.fa.gz', shell=True)
    subprocess.call('gunzip ./data/hg38.ml.fa.gz', shell=True)

fasta_open = pysam.Fastafile('./data/hg38.ml.fa')
seq = fasta_open.fetch('chr12', 115163136, 116211712).upper()
seq_1hot = dna_io.dna_1hot(seq)
test_pred_from_seq = seqnn_model.model.predict(np.expand_dims(seq_1hot,0))
print(test_pred_from_seq.shape)
PY

profile.summary: Puffin-D is a deep learning model that predicts transcription initiation signals from DNA sequence. It takes 100 kbp of genome sequence and returns base-level predictions for ten tracks: five assays that map transcription start sites (FANTOM CAGE, ENCODE CAGE, ENCODE RAMPAGE, GRO-cap and PRO-cap) on each strand. It is the prediction-focused companion of Puffin, an interpretable model from the same authors.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction; Puffin-D

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Puffin-D is a fully convolutional network. One-hot DNA passes through a stack of strided 1D convolutions that downsample the sequence by factors of 4, 4, 5, 5, 5 and 2, each followed by residual convolution blocks. Upsampling layers with skip connections then restore base resolution. This down-and-up pass is repeated a second time. A final 1x1 convolution with a softplus gives 10 non-negative output tracks at each position. Training details were not in the sources read.

sections.title: Puffin and Puffin-D
sections.body: The repository holds two models. Puffin is an interpretation-focused model that explains each transcription start site in terms of motifs and single bases, and works on short sequences with 325 bp padding on each side. Puffin-D is the deep learning model for prediction over 100 kbp. The README says Puffin-D gives better predictions when prediction is the main need.

profile.summary: DeepSTARR predicts how strongly a 249 base pair piece of DNA acts as an enhancer in Drosophila melanogaster S2 cells. It is a convolutional neural network with two outputs, one for developmental and one for housekeeping enhancer activity, trained on genome-wide UMI-STARR-seq measurements. Besides prediction, it is used to read out which nucleotides drive the predicted activity and so to study transcription factor motifs and their syntax.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: DeepSTARR, DeepSTARR model; preprint abstract; DeepSTARR.model.json: input layer and output layers

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The architecture is adapted from Basset: four convolutional layers, each followed by batch normalisation, a ReLU activation and max pooling, then two fully connected layers of 256 units and two single-unit output layers, Dense_Dev and Dense_Hk. The released model file gives 256 filters of width 7 in the first convolutional layer, then 60 of width 3, 60 of width 5 and 120 of width 3, with pooling size 2 throughout. The convolutional layers pick up local motifs and motif syntax; the fully connected layers combine them into one activity value per enhancer type. The model is a regression on measured UMI-STARR-seq activity, not a classifier.
sections.source_locator: README: DeepSTARR model; DeepSTARR.model.json: layers

sections.title: Interpreting the model
sections.body: The repository ships a second script that computes nucleotide contribution scores for a given sequence, separately for developmental or housekeeping activity, using DeepLIFT and SHAP. A Colab notebook runs the whole path end to end: training, contribution scores and TF-MoDISco motifs. The preprint states that the model learned TF motifs and higher-order syntax rules, including the effect of motif-flanking sequence and inter-motif distances, and that these rules were validated experimentally.
sections.source_locator: DeepSTARR/README.md: Interpreting DeepSTARR with nucleotide contribution scores, Tutorial; preprint abstract

The same record holds the train, validation and test sequences and their measured activities, so the published evaluation can be repeated. The model is also deposited in Kipoi. name: Orca
description: Orca 3D genome structure model.

version.note: Family record

profile.summary: Orca predicts the three-dimensional folding of the human genome from DNA sequence alone. It takes a genomic sequence of up to 256 Mb and returns predicted contact matrices at nine scales, from 4 kb resolution within 1 Mb up to whole-chromosome distances. It is used to run in silico Hi-C experiments: to ask what a structural variant, a haplotype or a designed sequence would do to local and large-scale genome structure.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: What is Orca, What can I use Orca for; paper: Results, Sequence-based prediction of multiscale 3D genome interactions

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Orca has a hierarchical sequence encoder and a cascade of decoders. The encoder turns a one-hot sequence into representations at nine resolutions, from 4 kb up to 1,024 kb. Each decoder predicts one 250 by 250 interaction matrix for a window of a given size, as a log fold change over a distance-based background. The decoders run from the top down: each lower level takes the sequence representation at its resolution, the prediction from the level above cropped and upsampled, and a pairwise distance encoding matrix. Encoder and decoders are convolutional with residual connections; each decoder has 112 convolution layers cycling through dilation factors 1 to 64. Predictions are symmetrised with their transpose and averaged between the forward and reverse-complement sequence. The encoder is also trained on an auxiliary task of predicting DNase-seq and ChIP-seq chromatin profiles.

name: BioFM
description: Transformer decoder genomic model whose BioToken tokeniser encodes variants and annotated regions alongside sequence, used to predict expression, splicing and variant pathogenicity.

profile.summary: BioFM is a genomic foundation model from M42 Health that reads DNA together with biological context. Its BioToken tokeniser encodes genetic variants and annotated regions (such as genes and regulatory elements) directly in the input, instead of treating DNA as bases only. The model produces embeddings for variants or sequences, which are used with simple classifiers to predict effects on expression, splicing and pathogenicity; it can also generate DNA sequence.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC abstract; model card: Model Details; README: Quick Start

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: BioFM is a decoder-only (causal) transformer on the Mistral architecture, with 23 layers and hidden size 640. Its input is DNA annotated with BioTokens: tokens that carry variant information and genomic annotations alongside the bases. For a variant, the package builds an upstream and a downstream sequence, each ending at the variant and half the evaluation context long; the downstream one is reverse complemented. Reference and mutated embeddings are each averaged over the two directions and then concatenated, giving a vector twice the embedding size. For plain sequences the embedding is taken from the last token. Downstream predictions use linear probing on these embeddings.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Model Details; config.json; README: Features, Creating Variant Embeddings, Sequence Embeddings, Prediction of Variant Effect

The README includes a script to reproduce the paper's variant benchmark by linear probing on the m42-health/variant-benchmark dataset with chromosome-based folds. Training ran on an NVIDIA DGX cluster with H100 GPUs using PyTorch FSDP.

steps.title: Extract sequence embeddings
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from biofm_eval import AnnotatedModel, AnnotationTokenizer, Embedder
import torch

MODEL_PATH = "m42-health/BioFM-265M"
TOKENIZER_PATH = "m42-health/BioFM-265M"

model = AnnotatedModel.from_pretrained(
    MODEL_PATH,
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)
tokenizer = AnnotationTokenizer.from_pretrained(TOKENIZER_PATH)

embedder = Embedder(model, tokenizer)

input_sequences = ['AGCT', 'GACTGCA']
sequence_embedding = embedder.get_sequence_embeddings(input_sequences)
print(f'Embedding dimension: {sequence_embedding.shape}')
PY
steps.explanation: The README's sequence embedding example, wrapped in a shell heredoc with its comments removed. It downloads BioFM-265M and needs no other input files.

description: Graph transformer DNA model that represents sequences with pan-genome and Minigraph graphs to capture population variation, with rotary position embeddings for sequences of varying length.

profile.summary: DeepGene is a DNA foundation model that learns from a pan-genome graph rather than a single reference sequence, so that genetic variation across individuals is part of what it sees in pretraining. It is a transformer encoder with rotary position embeddings, built to handle sequences of different lengths. The pretrained model is fine-tuned for sequence classification tasks such as promoter prediction and the Genome Understanding Evaluation (GUE) tasks.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model is a RoFormer, a transformer encoder with rotary position embeddings, pretrained as a masked language model. The code's default configuration has 12 layers, hidden size 768, 12 attention heads, a vocabulary of 4096 tokens and 5120 positions; pretraining builds the model from this default configuration. The pretraining data comes from a Minigraph pan-genome graph: the processing script reads the graph's sequence segments and edges and tokenises them with the repository's tokenizer.json, and pretraining uses subgraphs (default size 128). For downstream tasks the pretrained weights are loaded into a sequence classification model and fine-tuned, with MCC or F1 as the metric.

profile.summary: DNAGPT is a GPT-style DNA language model from Tencent AI Lab and collaborators. It reads a DNA sequence, split into 6-letter words, and can also take numbers as input; it can generate new DNA sequence, classify a sequence or predict a numerical value such as mRNA expression level. Pre-training adds two side tasks, predicting whether a sequence was reversed and predicting its GC content, to the usual next-token prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv v3: author affiliations; arXiv abstract; README.md: Test examples; test.py get_model

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DNAGPT is a decoder-only Transformer: the 0.1B model has 12 blocks of unidirectional attention, 12 heads each and a hidden size of 768. The DNA sequence is cut into non-overlapping k-mers, and numbers are encoded as separate number tokens; each token type has its own embedding layer and output head. Pre-training combines three tasks: next-token prediction, GC-content prediction for a random segment, and prediction of whether the sequence order was flipped. Reversing sequences lets the left-to-right model use context from both directions. For a downstream task the needed heads are kept and the model is fine-tuned.

name: eccDNAMamba
description: Bidirectional Mamba state-space encoder for full-length extrachromosomal circular DNA up to 200 kb, trained with an augmentation that preserves circular topology.

version.note: Family record; checkpoints are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Listed on the GENEB leaderboard as a genomic foundation model family.

profile.summary: eccDNAMamba is a pretrained model for extrachromosomal circular DNA (eccDNA), circular DNA molecules that carry amplified oncogenes in cancer. It reads full-length eccDNA sequences of 10 to 200 kbp, and copies the start of each sequence onto its end so the model sees across the point where the circle was opened. Fine-tuned versions are used for cancer-associated eccDNA prediction, copy-number level estimation, and telling real from pseudo-eccDNA.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; model card: Model Overview; inference_sample.py circular_augmentation

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: eccDNAMamba is a bidirectional state-space model: forward and reverse Mamba-2 encoders read the sequence in both directions, with cost linear in sequence length. DNA is tokenised by motif-level byte pair encoding (BPE) with a vocabulary of 4096. To respect the circular shape, a head-tail augmentation appends the first 64 tokens after the end of the sequence. The pretrained backbone is a masked language model (BiMambaForMaskedLM) with 24 layers and d_model 768. For classification, the published fine-tuning code mean-pools the hidden states and adds a two-layer classifier head.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Model Overview; arXiv abstract; config.json; inference_sample.py

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The pretrained backbone is eccDNAMamba/eccDNAMamba-1M (read at revision 36d95a3f). Seven fine-tuned checkpoints are published under the same organisation: cancer eccDNA prediction (short and ultra-long), copy-number level prediction (thresholds 10 and 4.5) and real against pseudo-eccDNA for Arabidopsis thaliana, Gallus gallus and Homo sapiens. The fine-tuned ultra-long checkpoint names eccDNAMamba-1M as its base model. A result should name the checkpoint and its revision. The repository also has a pretraining entry point (main.py).

name: Evo
description: StripedHyena DNA language models of 7 billion parameters (Evo 1 and Evo 1.5), trained at single-nucleotide resolution on prokaryotic and phage genomes with 8 kb or 131 kb contexts, for zero-shot function prediction and sequence generation.

version.note: Family record; checkpoints are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Listed on the GENEB leaderboard as a genomic foundation model family.

profile.summary: Evo is a 7-billion-parameter DNA language model trained on prokaryotic whole genomes. It reads DNA one base at a time, with a context of 8,192 or 131,072 bases depending on the checkpoint, and predicts the next base. The developers use it to score how likely a sequence is and to generate new DNA, from single genes and CRISPR-Cas systems up to genome-scale sequences.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction and checkpoint table; Usage

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Evo uses the StripedHyena architecture, a hybrid of multi-head attention and gated convolutions arranged in Hyena blocks. Hyena layers do most of the sequence processing and attention layers add targeted pattern recall, which gives near-linear scaling of compute and memory with context length. Tokens are single nucleotides (byte-level). The model is autoregressive: it outputs logits over the vocabulary at each position, which are used to sample new sequence or to score the log-likelihood of an existing one. Generation can run in a recurrent mode; the model card reports more than 500k bases generated on a single 80GB GPU.
sections.source_locator: README.md: introduction, Usage; model card: Model Architecture

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: evo-1-8k-base was pretrained at 8,192 context. evo-1-131k-base continues from it at 131,072 context. Evo 1.5 (evo-1.5-8k-base) extends the pretraining of evo-1-8k-base with 50% more data, to 450 billion tokens, and was introduced in a 2025 Nature paper. Two fine-tuned models generate CRISPR-Cas systems and IS200/IS605 transposons. The model card adds 15 intermediate pretraining checkpoints as branches. The Hugging Face weights had a projection-permutation bug that affects generation; the fix is loaded with revision="1.1_fix". The evo-model package had an inference bug in versions installed between Nov 15 and Dec 16, 2024, fixed from release 0.3. A result should name the checkpoint, the Hugging Face revision and the package version. The developers now point to Evo 2 as the successor.

model.eval()

sequence = 'ACGT'
input_ids = torch.tensor(
    tokenizer.tokenize(sequence),
    dtype=torch.int,
).to(device).unsqueeze(0)

with torch.no_grad():
    logits, _ = model(input_ids) # (batch, length, vocab)

print('Logits: ', logits)
print('Shape (batch, length, vocab): ', logits.shape)
PY

profile.summary: GENERator is a family of generative DNA language models: it reads a DNA sequence and predicts what comes next, so it can both generate new sequence and produce embeddings for downstream tasks. The models are Transformer decoders that read DNA in 6-letter chunks (6-mers), with a context of up to 98k base pairs. The first release was trained on 386 billion nucleotides of eukaryotic DNA; a second release (GENERator-v2) adds eukaryote and prokaryote models.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GENERator is a decoder-only Transformer trained as a causal language model on DNA: it predicts the next token from the tokens before it. DNA is split into 6-mer tokens. The first-release 1.2B checkpoint uses a Llama-type configuration with 26 layers, hidden size 2048, 32 attention heads and 4 key-value heads, a vocabulary of 4128 tokens and up to 16384 token positions. Embeddings are read from the last hidden layer, either at the last token or averaged over all tokens. GENERator-v2 adds a training objective that recovers single-nucleotide likelihoods from k-mer tokens, and pretraining data concentrated on gene-centric and regulatory regions.

steps.shell:

steps.title: Load the model and generate
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "GenerTeam/GENERator-eukaryote-1.2b-base",
    attn_implementation="flash_attention_2",
    trust_remote_code=True,
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
).cuda().eval()

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(
    "GenerTeam/GENERator-eukaryote-1.2b-base",
    trust_remote_code=True,
)

sequences = [
    "ATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCG",
    "ACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGT"
]

processed_sequences = ["<s>" + seq[len(seq)%6:] for seq in sequences]

inputs = tokenizer(
    processed_sequences,
    add_special_tokens=False,
    return_tensors="pt",
    padding=True,
    padding_side="left",
).to("cuda")

with torch.inference_mode():
    outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=32, do_sample=False)

decoded_sequences = tokenizer.batch_decode(outputs, skip_special_tokens=True)
print(decoded_sequences)
PY

profile.summary: GenomeOcean is a family of generative DNA language models trained on co-assembled environmental metagenomes, mainly microbial DNA. It reads DNA split into multi-base tokens and predicts the next token. The developers provide scripts to produce sequence embeddings for analysis and to generate new DNA from a prompt. The largest model has 4 billion parameters and reads up to about 50,000 bases.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GenomeOcean is a decoder-only transformer trained by causal language modelling: it predicts the next token from the tokens before it. DNA is split by a BPE tokenizer with 4096 tokens, so 1024 tokens cover about 5,100 bp. The 4B checkpoint uses the Mistral architecture in transformers, with 24 layers, hidden size 3072, 12 attention heads and 4 key/value heads. The package uses vLLM for fast generation and also produces sequence embeddings. The developers report that the embeddings capture phylogenetic and protein-coding structure.

sections.body: Three base models are published: GenomeOcean-100M and GenomeOcean-500M with a 1024-token context, and GenomeOcean-4B with a 10240-token context. Two fine-tuned 4B models exist: GenomeOcean-4B-bgcFM, trained on 11M biosynthetic gene cluster sequences, and GenomeOcean-4B-Artificial-Detector, a classifier for GenomeOcean-generated sequences. The developers recommend the 4B model for general use. The package recently moved to the vLLM V1 engine and transformers 5.12 or later; under transformers 5, the tokenizer should be loaded with PreTrainedTokenizerFast. A result should name the checkpoint, its Hugging Face revision, and the package commit; this page read GenomeOcean-4B at revision 2bed2fc3 and the code at commit 06fa4331.

name: genomics-fm
description: Transformer encoder pretrained on unlabelled genomes with an ensemble of tokenisation vocabularies, then fine-tuned with a task-specific vocabulary for annotation, profile and variant effect prediction.

version.note: Family record; checkpoints are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Listed on the GENEB leaderboard as a genomic foundation model family.

profile.summary: Genomics-FM is a DNA foundation model meant to cut the amount of labelled data that genomic prediction tasks need. It is a BERT-style encoder pretrained on large amounts of unlabelled DNA with an ensemble of tokenisation vocabularies (BPE and 6-mer), then fine-tuned with one task-specific vocabulary on a small labelled set. The authors apply it to genome annotation, epigenomic and expression profile prediction, and variant effect assessment.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC abstract; srun_pretrain.py; srun_pretrain.sh

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model is a BERT masked language model built on the MosaicML BERT code, which uses ALiBi position biases and FlashAttention. During pretraining each sequence is tokenised either with a BPE vocabulary or as 6-mers, and a prompt token marking the vocabulary ([BPE] or [KMER]) and the position scheme ([ALIBI] or [APE]) is put in front of it. Sequences are randomly replaced by their reverse complement half the time. Training masks tokens with a probability of 0.15 for BPE input and 0.15 divided by 6 for 6-mer input, over blocks of 512 tokens, for up to 1,000,000 steps in fp16. For a downstream task the model is fine-tuned with one chosen vocabulary.

name: GROVER
description: BERT-style DNA language model trained on the human genome with a byte-pair vocabulary chosen to carry the most sequence information, whose embeddings are fine-tuned for tasks such as promoter and protein-DNA binding prediction.

version.note: Family record; checkpoints are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Listed on the GENEB leaderboard as a genomic foundation model family.

profile.summary: GROVER is a DNA language model pretrained on the human genome. It splits DNA into variable-length tokens learned by byte-pair encoding, and turns a DNA sequence into contextual embeddings. Its authors intend it as a foundation model that is fine-tuned for a specific task, such as promoter identity or protein-DNA binding.
profile.summary_source_locator: bioRxiv abstract; tutorial notebook, Overview

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GROVER is a BERT model for masked language modelling: 12 layers, hidden size 768, 12 attention heads and a vocabulary of 609 tokens. The vocabulary comes from byte-pair encoding of the human genome, and the authors chose the vocabulary size with a next-k-mer prediction task. Because byte-pair tokens depend on the surrounding sequence, a short sequence can be tokenised differently from the same stretch in the whole genome; the card advises adding 100 nucleotides at each end. For a task, the pretrained model is loaded with a classification head and fine-tuned on labelled sequences.

strengths.text: Loads with standard Hugging Face transformers classes, and the authors publish an end-to-end fine-tuning tutorial.
The tokenised human genome is published with nucleotide mappers, so tokens can be traced back to genome positions.
The tutorial runs fine-tuning on a free Colab T4 GPU, though the authors warn training there may take a while.

limitations.text: Trained on the human genome only.
Tokenisation depends on sequence context: sequences under 50 nucleotides are tokenised differently, and sequence edges need care, so short inputs need flanking sequence.
The context is 512 tokens, not nucleotides; the authors' tutorial works with sequences of about 1 kb truncated to 310 tokens. Long-range inputs are not supported by this configuration.
The Hugging Face card states no licence; only the Zenodo copy carries CC-BY-4.0. Fine-tuning needs a GPU according to the tutorial.

steps.title: Fine-tune on the CTCF example and evaluate
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import pandas as pd
import wget
import os
import numpy as np

from sklearn.metrics import matthews_corrcoef, accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score

import transformers
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, Trainer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification, TrainingArguments
from torch.utils.data import Dataset

CTCF_dataset_url = "https://datashare.tu-dresden.de/s/pjb5gcWGGrbcARN/download/CTCF_dataset.tsv"
file_name = "CTCF_dataset.tsv"
if os.path.exists(file_name):
  os.remove(file_name) # if exists, remove it directly
file_name = wget.download(CTCF_dataset_url, out=file_name)

CTCF_dataset = pd.read_csv('CTCF_dataset.tsv', sep='\t')
train = CTCF_dataset.sample(frac=0.8, random_state=0)
validation = CTCF_dataset.drop(train.index)
test = validation.sample(frac=0.5, random_state=0)
validation = validation.drop(test.index)
train = train.reset_index(drop=True)
validation = validation.reset_index(drop=True)
test = test.reset_index(drop=True)

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("PoetschLab/GROVER")
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("PoetschLab/GROVER")

class SupervisedDataset(Dataset):
    """Dataset for supervised fine-tuning."""
    def __init__(self, texts, labels, tokenizer):
        super(SupervisedDataset, self).__init__()
        sequences = [text for text in texts]
        output = tokenizer(
            sequences,
            add_special_tokens=True,
            max_length=310,
            padding="longest",
            return_tensors="pt",
            truncation=True
        )
        self.input_ids = output["input_ids"]
        self.attention_mask = output["attention_mask"]
        self.labels = labels
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.input_ids)
    def __getitem__(self, i):
        return dict(
            input_ids=self.input_ids[i],
            labels=self.labels[i],
            attention_mask=self.attention_mask[i]
        )

train_dataset = SupervisedDataset(train.sequence, train.label, tokenizer)
test_dataset = SupervisedDataset(test.sequence, test.label, tokenizer)
val_dataset = SupervisedDataset(validation.sequence, validation.label, tokenizer)

def calculate_metric_with_sklearn(logits: np.ndarray, labels: np.ndarray):
    predictions = np.argmax(logits, axis=-1)
    return {
        "accuracy": accuracy_score(labels, predictions),
        "f1": f1_score(labels, predictions, average="macro", zero_division=0),
        "matthews_correlation": matthews_corrcoef(labels, predictions),
        "precision": precision_score(labels, predictions, average="macro", zero_division=0),
        "recall": recall_score(labels, predictions, average="macro", zero_division=0),
    }

def compute_metrics(eval_pred):
    logits, labels = eval_pred
    if isinstance(logits, tuple):  # Unpack logits if it's a tuple
        logits = logits[0]
    return calculate_metric_with_sklearn(logits, labels)

train_args = TrainingArguments(seed = 42,
                               output_dir=".",
                               per_device_train_batch_size=16,
                               eval_strategy="epoch",
                               learning_rate=0.000001,
                               num_train_epochs=4
                               )
trainer = transformers.Trainer(
                                model=model,
                                tokenizer=tokenizer,
                                compute_metrics=compute_metrics,
                                train_dataset=train_dataset,
                                eval_dataset=val_dataset,
                                args = train_args
                                )
trainer.train()
results = trainer.evaluate(eval_dataset=test_dataset)
print(results)
PY

name: JanusDNA
description: Hybrid Mamba, attention and mixture-of-experts DNA model that combines autoregressive and masked pretraining to read sequences of up to 1 Mb in both directions at single-nucleotide resolution.

version.note: Family record; checkpoints are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Listed on the GENEB leaderboard as a genomic foundation model family.

profile.summary: JanusDNA is a DNA language model that reads sequence one nucleotide at a time and is designed for long inputs. It is pre-trained on the human reference genome so that each position is predicted from the sequence on both sides of it, and its learned representations are then fine-tuned for tasks such as regulatory element classification and eQTL prediction. The models are small: the README lists sizes of 1.980M to 2.009M and 7.662M parameters.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; arXiv v4: Section 4.1, Table 9; README.md: Reproducing Experiments

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The input sequence is encoded by two independent stacks, one reading left to right and one right to left. Each stack has 8 layers, each with a Mamba block and a feed-forward block, and half of the feed-forward blocks are replaced by mixture-of-experts blocks with 16 experts. A final fusion layer, a FlexAttention layer with 4 heads, joins the two directions with an attention mask that lets the prediction for a position see the left context from the forward pass and the right context from the backward pass, but not the position itself. This lets every token contribute to the loss, as in autoregressive training, while the model still learns from both sides, as in masked training. One variant also replaces the Mamba block in the fifth layer with a causal attention layer (mid-attention). A later update adds two MLP layers after the fusion layer.
sections.source_locator: arXiv v4: Section 3.1; Appendix B.2.1 Architecture configuration; README.md: Update 2025-08-01

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper pre-trains three widths: hidden size 32 and 72 for 1,024-nucleotide inputs (10,000 steps), and 144 for 131,072-nucleotide inputs (50,000 steps). The 32 and 72 widths come with and without mid-attention. The weights dataset on Harvard Dataverse (version 2) holds five original checkpoints with their configuration files and five later checkpoints with the final MLP layers (JanusDNA_mlp), which the README calls the latest. The GenomicBenchmarks script expects a pretrained checkpoint under outputs/pretrain/hg38/, in a folder named after its configuration. A result should give the width, the input length, whether mid-attention was used and whether the final MLP was used.
sections.source_locator: arXiv v4: Appendix B.2.1 Pre-training setup; Dataverse file list; README.md: Update

sections.title: Setting up the code
sections.body: The README covers environment setup and scripts that reproduce the paper: pre-training on hg38 and fine-tuning on GenomicBenchmarks, the Nucleotide Transformer tasks and the DNALongBench eQTL tasks. Setup uses a conda environment file and a prebuilt Mamba wheel for CUDA 12, PyTorch 2.5 and Python 3.11 on Linux x86_64. The scripts contain placeholder paths to fill in, and the GenomicBenchmarks script is written for 8 GPUs. The README gives no example of loading a checkpoint and embedding a single sequence.

name: LucaOne
description: Transformer encoder pretrained jointly on nucleic acid and protein sequences from about 170,000 species, giving one representation for DNA, RNA and protein inputs.

version.note: Family record; checkpoints are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Listed on the GENEB leaderboard as a genomic foundation model family.

profile.summary: LucaOne is a biological foundation model that reads nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) and protein sequences with one shared model. Given a sequence and its type, it returns an embedding: a matrix with one vector per residue or a single vector for the whole sequence. These embeddings are used as inputs to downstream models for sequence-level or residue-level classification and regression.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: title, TimeLine 2025/12/31; LucaOneApp README: embedding methods and parameters

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LucaOne (also called LucaGPLM) is a transformer encoder over a joint vocabulary of nucleotides and amino acids. The published checkpoint has a masked language model head, which the developers describe as for pre-training and sequence recovery; the full set of pretraining tasks is described in the paper, which was not read. The published default checkpoint has 20 layers, hidden size 2560, 40 attention heads and a 39-token vocabulary, with no absolute position embeddings. Each input is marked as gene (DNA or RNA) or prot. The output is the last hidden layer: per-token vectors including [CLS] and [SEP], which can be pooled to one vector by mean, [CLS] or trainable attention pooling. Long sequences are split into overlapping fragments and the embeddings merged.
sections.source_locator: model card: Usage; config.json; LucaOneApp README: embedding methods, notes

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Checkpoints are named by training step. The README recommends lucaone at step 36000000, 17600000 or 5600000 for both nucleic acid and protein, lucaone-gene at step 36800000 for DNA and RNA only, and lucaone-prot at step 30000000 for protein only. The original code downloads them from the developers' FTP server by --llm_type, --llm_version and --llm_step. Since 2025 they are also on Hugging Face under LucaGroup, loaded with the lucaone package (version 1.1.1 for the card read). A result should name the checkpoint and step, the route (FTP code or Hugging Face) and the Hugging Face revision; this page read LucaOne-default-step36M at revision f0d2807e.

run_guide.summary: Install the lucaone package with the pinned tokenizers and transformers versions, load LucaOne-default-step36M from Hugging Face and embed a short nucleotide sequence.
prerequisites: Python with pip. The original repository uses Python 3.9.13; the model card does not state a Python version.
A GPU is used if available, otherwise CPU. The developers advise a large-memory GPU such as an A100 for long sequences.
Weights are MIT licensed on the model card; code is Apache-2.0. The weights are not gated.

steps.title: Install the package
steps.shell:
pip install lucaone==1.1.1
pip install tokenizers==0.19.1
pip install transformers==4.41.2
steps.explanation: The model card's install commands.

steps.title: Embed a nucleotide sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
import lucaone
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel, TrainingArguments, Trainer

# model_id
model_id = "LucaGroup/LucaOne-default-step36M"

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    trust_remote_code=True,
    force_download=True
)

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    task_level="token_level",
    task_type="embedding",
    trust_remote_code=True,
    force_download=True
)

# device
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
model.to(device)
model.eval()

# nucleotide sequence
nucleotide_sequence = "ATGCGTACGTTAGC"
nucleotide_inputs = tokenizer(
    nucleotide_sequence,
    # note: gene sequence(for DNA or RNA), seq_type must be 'gene'
    seq_type="gene",
    return_tensors="pt",
    add_special_tokens=True
)
new_nucleotide_inputs = {}
for item in nucleotide_inputs.items():
    new_nucleotide_inputs[item[0]] = item[1].to(device)
nucleotide_inputs = new_nucleotide_inputs

with torch.no_grad():
    nucleotide_outputs = model(**nucleotide_inputs)
    # last hidden matrix as embedding matrix: [batch_size, seq_len + 2, hidden_size]
    nucleotide_last_hidden = nucleotide_outputs.last_hidden_state
    # mean pooling
    mean_nucleotide_embedding = nucleotide_last_hidden[:, 1:-1, :].mean(dim=1)
print(f"Nucleotide Embedding Shape: {nucleotide_last_hidden.shape}")
print(mean_nucleotide_embedding)
PY
steps.explanation: The model card's feature-extraction example, wrapped in a shell heredoc and shortened: the protein half and some intermediate print lines are left out. Use seq_type="prot" for a protein sequence, as the card shows.

outputs: The shape of the embedding matrix, [batch_size, seq_len + 2, hidden_size], and the mean-pooled embedding vector.
limitations: These commands were read from the model card and have not been executed by Rewire.
force_download=True downloads the weights again on every run.
For long sequences or batch embedding to files, the developers point to the LucaOneApp repository instead.

name: MutBERT
description: Masked DNA language model that represents the human genome as allele-frequency distributions from population data, so pretraining concentrates on sites of variation.

version.note: Family record; checkpoints are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Listed on the GENEB leaderboard as a genomic foundation model family.

profile.summary: MutBERT is a DNA language model for the human genome that is built to learn from genetic variation such as single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Instead of training on one reference sequence, it encodes each genome position as a probability over the four bases, taken from allele frequencies in the 1000 Genomes Project. Given a DNA sequence, it outputs per-nucleotide embeddings that can be pooled into a sequence embedding or fine-tuned for classification.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; 2.2 Probabilistic genome representation; README: 4.2 Get the embeddings

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MutBERT is a transformer encoder trained with masked language modelling. It has 12 encoder layers and uses rotary position embeddings (RoPE) and flash attention. Each position in the input is a distribution over the bases: positions without observed variants give the reference base a probability of 1, and variable positions carry the observed allele frequencies. Because the input is a probability matrix and not a token sequence, the usual embedding look-up is replaced by a linear layer, so each position's embedding is a weighted sum of the base embeddings. During pretraining the authors apply temperature scaling to the skewed allele probabilities. The model works at single-nucleotide level with a vocabulary of A, T, C, G and five special tokens. In the README usage example, plain sequences are passed as a one-hot matrix.
sections.source_locator: Paper: 2.1 Model architecture, 2.2 Probabilistic genome representation, 2.3 Tokenization and vocabulary, 2.4; README: 4.2 Get the embeddings

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three pretrained checkpoints share one architecture and differ only in the training data. MutBERT uses probabilistic genomes from the 1000 Genomes Project. MutBERT-Multi uses probabilistic genomes from a 100-species whole-genome alignment. MutBERT-Ref (on Hugging Face, CompBioDSA/MutBERT-Human-Ref) takes one-hot encodings of the hg38 reference and serves as the deterministic baseline. All were trained for 120 000 steps with batch size 2048 and maximum sequence length 512. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision; this page read MutBERT at a6cdc94d, MutBERT-Human-Ref at 766be54e and MutBERT-Multi at cbdab668.
sections.source_locator: Paper: 2.1 Model architecture, 2.4 to 2.5; README: 2. Model and Results; model cards: title lines

sections.title: Evaluation in the paper
sections.body: The authors compared MutBERT with DNABERT-2, several Nucleotide Transformer versions and modified MutBERT variants on transcription factor binding sites (from the GUE benchmark), the Nucleotide Transformer downstream tasks and eQTL variant effect prediction. For the eQTL task they extended MutBERT's input from 512 to 2048 base pairs and trained an SVM on the embeddings. The authors report that MutBERT ranked among the top models, and that it beat the alternatives in most of the three eQTL distance categories. They note it was pretrained on 4 L20 GPUs for 6 days.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; 2.7 Downstream tasks; 3.2 eQTL variant effect prediction; Discussion; README: 6. Finetune

strengths.text: Uses population variation directly: the input encodes observed allele frequencies, so pretraining concentrates on sites where people differ.
A matched reference-only checkpoint (MutBERT-Ref) with the same architecture is released, so a user can test whether variation-aware training helps on their own task.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: 2.1 Model architecture; MutBERT-Human-Ref model card

strengths.text: Small and cheap to train by the authors' account: 86 million parameters, pretrained on 4 L20 GPUs in 6 days.
Loads through the Hugging Face transformers library, with MIT-licensed weights and the pretraining and fine-tuning code in the repository.

limitations.text: Short pretraining context of 512 nucleotides. Longer inputs rely on RoPE extension.

limitations.text: Each position is encoded independently, so co-variation between nearby variants is not captured. The authors say this is why MutBERT did worse on multi-species data than on 1000 Genomes data, and that its behaviour on denser variant sets such as gnomAD is untested.
The model takes a matrix over the vocabulary, not token IDs, and loading runs custom code from the Hugging Face repository (trust_remote_code=True).

run_guide.summary: Set up the repository environment at a pinned commit, download MutBERT from Hugging Face and compute a mean-pooled and a max-pooled embedding for a short DNA sequence.
prerequisites: conda, to create a Python 3.12 environment.
The requirements file pins torch==2.5.1 and transformers==4.45.2. The README example runs on CPU; GPU type and memory for inference are not stated.
Weights are MIT licensed and not gated. The code repository states no licence.
Loading needs trust_remote_code=True, which runs the model code shipped in the Hugging Face repository.

steps.title: Compute an embedding
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel

model_name = "CompBioDSA/MutBERT"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(model_name, trust_remote_code=True)

dna = "ATCGGGGCCCATTA"
inputs = tokenizer(dna, return_tensors='pt')["input_ids"]

mut_inputs = F.one_hot(inputs, num_classes=len(tokenizer)).float().to("cpu")  # len(tokenizer) is vocab size
last_hidden_state = model(mut_inputs).last_hidden_state   # [1, sequence_length, 768]

# embedding with mean pooling
embedding_mean = torch.mean(last_hidden_state[0], dim=0)
print(embedding_mean.shape) # expect to be 768

# embedding with max pooling
embedding_max = torch.max(last_hidden_state[0], dim=0)[0]
print(embedding_max.shape) # expect to be 768
PY
steps.explanation: The README 'Get the embeddings' example wrapped in a shell heredoc, with its two comment-only alternative lines left out. It downloads the tokenizer and weights, one-hot encodes the tokens and runs the encoder. For the other checkpoints, change model_name to CompBioDSA/MutBERT-Human-Ref or CompBioDSA/MutBERT-Multi as the README lists them.

name: OmniNA
description: Generative nucleotide model pretrained on 91.7 million sequences with their text annotations from many species, fine-tuned to answer sequence tasks in natural language.

version.note: Family record; checkpoints are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Listed on the GENEB leaderboard as a genomic foundation model family.

profile.summary: OmniNA is a generative foundation model for nucleotide sequences from many species. It was pretrained on 91.7 million DNA and RNA sequences from the NCBI nucleotide database, each paired with its text annotation, so that it learns to write an annotation for a sequence. After fine-tuning, it answers questions about an input sequence in natural language, for example whether it is a promoter, or which species it comes from.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods, Data processing for OmniNA pre-training; README: Overview, Prepare Data

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: OmniNA uses the LLaMA architecture, an auto-regressive decoder-only transformer. Sequences and annotations share one byte pair encoding tokenizer, built with SentencePiece and trained on nucleotide sequences and wiki-103 text, with 32,001 tokens. Each pretraining example is a prompt with three parts: an instruction, a nucleotide sequence and its annotation, and the model is trained to generate the text. Inputs are capped at 601 tokens. Fine-tuning casts each downstream task as a question and answer: the training file adds a question column, and the model learns to generate the answer.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model architecture and pre-training; Data processing; Figure 1 caption; README: Prepare Data

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper and README describe three sizes. The README table gives OmniNA-66M (8 layers, 8 heads, 66 million parameters), OmniNA-330M (16 layers, 16 heads, 330 million) and OmniNA-1.7B (24 layers, 32 heads, 1.7 billion). Hugging Face holds XLS/OmniNA-66m, XLS/OmniNA-220m and XLS/OmniNA-1.7B. The XLS/OmniNA-220m configuration has 16 layers and 16 heads, the shape the README gives for OmniNA-330M, so the middle checkpoint appears to be the same model under two different size names. The model card read (1.7B) holds only a licence tag. A result should name the Hugging Face checkpoint and revision; this page read 66m at 2c5e876a, 220m at 64ea6ce7 and 1.7B at 73d208a3.
sections.source_locator: README: Model Variants, Installation; config.json of each checkpoint; Hugging Face listing; Paper: Results

sections.title: Evaluation in the paper
sections.body: The authors fine-tuned OmniNA on 17 tasks covering sequence detection (taxonomy classification through genomic element detection) and species classification, and report that OmniNA-1.7B surpasses or rivals the compared methods. They also apply it to the effect of mutations on DNA and RNA processing. The authors themselves warn that test sets may overlap the training data of the compared models, and that converting regression baselines to classification may bias the comparison.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Figure 1 caption; Discussion

name: PlantCaduceus
description: Caduceus and Mamba DNA language model pretrained on 16 angiosperm genomes, fine-tuned to predict translation start and stop sites and splice sites across plant species and to score deleterious variants.

version.note: Family record; checkpoints are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Listed on the GENEB leaderboard as a genomic foundation model family.

profile.summary: PlantCaduceus (short name PlantCAD) is a DNA language model for flowering plants, pretrained on the genomes of 16 angiosperm species. It reads 512-bp DNA windows one nucleotide at a time, looking at both strands. Its embeddings feed small classifiers that predict translation start and stop sites and splice sites in species it was not trained on, and its masked-base likelihoods give a zero-shot score for how deleterious a single-nucleotide variant is.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: PlantCAD overview; Paper: Abstract, Introduction, Fig. 1 caption

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: PlantCaduceus uses the Caduceus architecture, which builds on the Mamba state-space sequence model and adds bi-directionality and reverse complement (RC) equivariance, so both DNA strands are modelled together. It uses single-nucleotide tokens. Pretraining is masked language modelling: 15% of positions in each 512-bp window are masked and the model is trained with cross-entropy loss on them. Following GPN, the pretraining set down-samples noncoding regions and down-weights repeats. Downstream, frozen embeddings train XGBoost or linear classifiers, and the zero-shot score is the log-likelihood difference between the reference and alternate allele at a masked position.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Fig. 1 caption; Results; Methods; README: PlantCAD overview

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: PlantCAD comes in four sizes, named by their number of Caduceus blocks: PlantCaduceus_l20, l24, l28 and l32, all with a 512-bp input. The model card recommends the largest, l32, for zero-shot scoring. The same repository now also hosts PlantCAD2, a later generation with an 8192-bp input and separate checkpoints (Small, Medium, Large); it is a different model and is not covered here. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision; the listing read on 2026-11-26 gives l32 at e624c13c, l28 at 5ac1d5e7, l24 at 8c41e4d5 and l20 at d1b3c7d4.
sections.source_locator: README: Model summary; model card: Model Overview; Hugging Face listing; Paper: Results, Table 1

sections.title: Evaluation in the paper
sections.body: The authors trained XGBoost and linear classifiers on Arabidopsis labels for translation initiation and termination sites and splice donor and acceptor sites, then tested them on species in the pretraining set (Oryza sativa, Sorghum bicolor) and outside it (Gossypium hirsutum, Glycine max, Zea mays). They compared PlantCaduceus with other DNA language models including GPN and AgroNT. For variants, they compared zero-shot scores with phyloP, phastCons, GPN and AgroNT. The claim of best cross-species performance is the authors'.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results; README: PlantCAD overview

steps.title: Compute embeddings
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForMaskedLM

device = 'cuda:0'
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('kuleshov-group/PlantCaduceus_l32')
model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained(
    'kuleshov-group/PlantCaduceus_l32', trust_remote_code=True
).to(device)

sequence = ""

input_ids = tokenizer.encode_plus(
    sequence, return_tensors="pt", return_attention_mask=False,
    return_token_type_ids=False
)["input_ids"].to(device)

with torch.inference_mode():
    outputs = model(input_ids=input_ids, output_hidden_states=True)

embeddings = outputs.hidden_states[-1].to(torch.float32).cpu().numpy()

# Average forward and reverse complement embeddings
hidden_size = embeddings.shape[-1] // 2
forward = embeddings[..., 0:hidden_size]
reverse = embeddings[..., hidden_size:][:, ::-1, :]
averaged_embeddings = (forward + reverse) / 2
print(averaged_embeddings.shape)
PY
steps.explanation: The README 'Quick example' wrapped in a shell heredoc. It downloads PlantCaduceus_l32, runs one 512-bp sequence on the GPU and averages the forward and reverse-complement halves of the last hidden state.

outputs: The shape of the strand-averaged embedding array: one row per token of the input sequence, with half the width of the raw hidden state. The README does not print the expected numbers.

name: SPACE
description: Supervised DNA model that learns sequence representations by predicting genomic profiles such as chromatin accessibility across species, using species- and profile-specific mixture-of-experts layers.

version.note: Family record; checkpoints are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Listed on the GENEB leaderboard as a genomic foundation model family.

profile.summary: SPACE is a DNA model that learns sequence representations by supervised training rather than by masked or next-token prediction. It is trained to predict thousands of genomic profiles, such as chromatin accessibility, transcription factor binding, histone marks and CAGE, from long human and mouse DNA sequences. Its encoder can then be fine-tuned or used as a feature extractor for other DNA tasks, and the full model predicts the profiles themselves.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; 4.1 Pre-training; README: Try the Genomic Profile Prediction, Downstream Tasks

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SPACE (Species-Profile Adaptive Collaborative Experts) keeps the Enformer setup of predicting genomic profiles from DNA, and adds two Mixture of Experts (MoE) parts. A species-aware encoder adds a trainable species embedding and routes each input sparsely across experts, so it can learn both species-specific and shared features. A profile-grouped enhancement decoder uses gated experts to model dependencies between profile types before the human and mouse output heads. The implementation is based on Enformer-Pytorch and Mod-Squad. In the released configuration the input is 131,072 bp, the model width is 1536 with 11 layers and 8 attention heads, the species MoE has 4 experts and the profile MoE has 8, and topk is set to 3.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; 3 Method; README: Acknowledgments; config.json

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The README names one pretrained checkpoint, yangyz1230/space on Hugging Face, which appears to be the paper's SPACE (large). Smaller variants in the paper (hidden size 768) were built only for ablation studies, and the README names none of them. The training data are the Enformer human and mouse sets, which the authors converted from the Basenji TensorFlow files to H5 and published as the Hugging Face dataset yangyz1230/space. A result should name the checkpoint revision; this page read revision 63c9f501.
sections.source_locator: README: Pre-trained Model, Dataset; Paper: Appendix H; Hugging Face API response

sections.title: Evaluation in the paper
sections.body: The authors fine-tuned the encoder on the Nucleotide Transformer downstream tasks, where they report the best result on 11 of 18 tasks, including against the 2.5B-parameter NT-Multispecies model, and they compare with Enformer on the GUE benchmark. With frozen embeddings on the BEND benchmark they report strong results on chromatin accessibility, histone modification and CpG methylation, but limited effectiveness on the two variant effect tasks. These are the authors' own results.

profile.summary: AIDO.DNA, now renamed GB.DNA by its developer GenBio AI, is a large DNA language model meant as a general-purpose encoder of DNA sequence. It reads up to 4,000 nucleotides one base at a time and was pretrained on 10.6 billion nucleotides from 796 species. Its embeddings are fine-tuned or probed for tasks such as gene expression prediction, genome mining, in silico mutagenesis and sequence generation.
profile.summary_source_locator: bioRxiv abstract; model card: introduction, Tokenization; ModelGenerator backbones: deprecated aliases

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: AIDO.DNA is a BERT-style, encoder-only dense transformer trained with masked language modelling. It uses single-nucleotide tokens from a 5-letter vocabulary (A, T, C, G, N), with a [CLS] token at the start and an [EOS] token at the end of each sequence. The authors updated the BERT design with SwiGLU, LayerNorms and rotary positional embeddings (RoPE). The 7B model has 32 layers, 32 attention heads and hidden size 4352. Its design bet, in the authors' words, is to scale model size while keeping a short 4k context. It was trained for 100000 iterations at global batch size 1024 on 256 H100 GPUs with Megatron-LM, which took 8 days.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Model Architectural Details, Tokenization, Training Details; bioRxiv abstract

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two pretrained checkpoints are released: a 7B model and a 300M model. Both were first published as AIDO.DNA-7B and AIDO.DNA-300M and are now named GB.DNA-7B and GB.DNA-300M on Hugging Face; the old names still resolve to the new repositories. In ModelGenerator the backbones are gb_dna_7b and gb_dna_300m, and the old names aido_dna_7b and aido_dna_300m remain as deprecated aliases. The 300M card gives no training details of its own and refers to the 7B card. A result should name the checkpoint and its revision; this page read GB.DNA-7B at 5dd948f7 and GB.DNA-300M at a833c560.
sections.source_locator: Hugging Face API responses (requested by old name); ModelGenerator backbones; 300M model card

sections.title: Evaluation in the paper
sections.body: The authors evaluated the 7B model on supervised, generative and zero-shot tasks in functional genomics, synthetic biology and drug development, choosing hyperparameters on a 10% validation split. They report that it outperforms earlier encoder-only DNA models without using new data, and argue that new scaling laws are needed for compute-optimal DNA language models. These are the authors' claims; only the abstract and model card were read.

profile.summary: Enigma is a sequence-to-function model for regulatory genomics from Deep Genomics. It reads a long stretch of DNA and predicts genome tracks such as RNA-seq, DNase-seq and ATAC-seq signal at single-base resolution. Enigma-Distilled is the released pretrained checkpoint, a distilled model provided for non-commercial use.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Enigma takes a one-hot DNA sequence and predicts many genome tracks at once, with a separate output head for human (hg38) and mouse (mm10). The default configuration in the code combines a U-Net with 7 downsampling steps and an 8-layer transformer of width 1536 that uses rotary position embeddings and FlashAttention, with prediction resolution 1. The authors' stated aim was efficiency: a smaller, curated set of training tracks and a cheaper architecture rather than a larger model. The released checkpoint is a distilled model, which GUANinE v1.1 describes as ensemble-distilled. The distillation procedure itself was not in the sources read.

name: ESA-dna2vec
description: ESA-dna2vec DNA embedding model.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: ESA-dna2vec is the DNA embedding model from the Embed-Search-Align (ESA) work, which treats read alignment as a search problem. A transformer encoder turns a DNA read or a reference genome fragment into a single vector, so that a read lands close to the fragment it came from. Reads are then aligned by searching a vector store of reference fragment embeddings and refining the best hits with Smith-Waterman scoring.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Figure 3 caption. Model card: Model Overview. GUANinE: list of evaluated models

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model, called the Reference-Free DNA Embedding (RDE) model in the paper, is a transformer encoder with 12 heads, 6 encoder layers, a vocabulary of 10,000 tokens and 1020-dimensional output vectors. It is trained self-supervised with a contrastive loss: a read sampled from a reference fragment is pulled towards that fragment's embedding and pushed away from a batch of random fragments. The card describes fragments of 800 to 2000 bases, reads of 150 to 500 bases, and 1 to 5% random base substitutions added to 40% of training reads. For alignment, the reference genome is cut into overlapping fragments, each fragment is embedded and stored in a vector database, and each read retrieves its top-K nearest fragments per chromosome before Smith-Waterman scoring picks the best location.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sec. 2.4 RDE encoder implementation; Sec. 2.5 retrieval and fine-alignment; Figure 2 caption. Model card: Model Architecture; Training Procedure

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint is on Hugging Face as roychowdhuryresearch/dna2vec; this page read revision 6e15acaa. It loads through transformers with custom model code from the repository (trust_remote_code=True), and the card adds a mean-pooling step over the last hidden state to get one vector per sequence. The paper says model checkpoints are also on OSF, and the training code is in a co-author's repository, KennethEnevoldsen/dna2vec, whose readme calls it DNA-ESA. The GUANinE benchmark lists the model as the contrastive dna2vec of Embed-Search-Align but the sources read do not say which copy it used. steps.title: Embed a sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

def load_hf_model():
    hf_model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("roychowdhuryresearch/dna2vec", trust_remote_code=True)
    hf_tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("roychowdhuryresearch/dna2vec", trust_remote_code=True)

    class AveragePooler(nn.Module):
        def forward(self, last_hidden, attention_mask):
            return (last_hidden * attention_mask.unsqueeze(-1)).sum(1) / attention_mask.sum(-1).unsqueeze(-1)

    hf_model.pooler = AveragePooler()
    return hf_model, hf_tokenizer, hf_model.pooler

def get_embedding(dna_sequence):
    model, tokenizer, pooler = load_hf_model()
    tokenized_input = tokenizer(dna_sequence, return_tensors="pt", padding=True)
    with torch.no_grad():
        output = model(**tokenized_input)
    embedding = pooler(output.last_hidden_state, tokenized_input.attention_mask)
    return embedding.numpy()

dna_seq = "ATGCGTACGTAGCTAGCTAGC"
embedding = get_embedding(dna_seq)
print("Embedding shape:", embedding.shape)
PY

profile.summary: hgT5 is a set of T5 transformer models pretrained on the human genome by the authors of the GUANinE benchmark. The models read DNA sequences of about 512 bp, split into learned tokens, and were fine-tuned separately on each GUANinE task, such as chromatin accessibility, sequence conservation and yeast promoter expression. They were built to test how self-supervised pretraining helps on these tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: GUANinE v1.0: Abstract; section 3.3 Novel Neural Baselines; Appendix E

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: hgT5 uses the T5 encoder-decoder transformer at 770 M parameters. DNA is split into tokens with a unigram language model tokenizer, with vocabularies of 512+3, 2048+3 or 8192+3 tokens. The models were pretrained on the human genome with T5's span-corruption objective, using 15% noise density and a mean span length of 3 tokens, then fine-tuned on each benchmark task separately. Matching T5 models without pretraining were trained as a comparison.
sections.source_locator: GUANinE v1.0: section 3.3; Appendix E

sections.title: Pretraining corpus
sections.body: The pretraining corpus is a reduced copy of hg38. The authors removed N-rich and repeat-rich regions and near-duplicate segments, which left 1.64 Gbp. They then made upsampled versions in which minor alleles from 1000 Genomes Project Phase 3 (allele frequency 1e-3 or greater) were inserted at random, to reduce reference bias.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three hgT5 models exist, named by vocabulary size: hgT5-515, hgT5-2051 and hgT5-8195. The authors trained three pretraining replicates of each and kept two. Each was then fine-tuned per task, so a published score refers to a task-specific fine-tuned model. GUANinE v1.1 re-reports hgT5-8195. profile.summary: Mistral-DNA is a family of DNA language models built by shrinking the Mixtral-8x7B mixture-of-experts architecture so it fits on a single GPU. The published checkpoints were pretrained on genome sequences, several on the human hg38 assembly and others on yeast, bacteria, viruses, plants and farm animals. A checkpoint takes a DNA sequence and returns per-token hidden states, which are pooled into an embedding or fine-tuned for a classification task.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: Overview; model card: Model Card, Calculate the embedding; Hugging Face listing

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each checkpoint is a Mixtral-style model: the card lists grouped-query attention, sliding-window attention, a byte-fallback BPE tokenizer and mixture of experts. The 138M human checkpoint's config gives 8 layers, hidden size 768, 8 attention heads, 8 key-value heads, 8 local experts with 1 expert used per token, a vocabulary of 4096 and max_position_embeddings 512, with sliding_window set to null. Its architecture entry is MixtralForCausalLM. In use, the card takes the hidden states returned by the model and max-pools them into one vector per sequence.

prerequisites: Python with pip, PyTorch and transformers. The model card says to use transformers 4.34.0 or newer.
The card's example does not require a GPU. The README's own training setup used an NVIDIA driver 535.129.03 with CUDA 12.2, and says the model was shrunk to train on a GPU such as an RTX3090.

steps.title: Load the model and embed a sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("RaphaelMourad/Mistral-DNA-v1-138M-hg38", trust_remote_code=True)
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("RaphaelMourad/Mistral-DNA-v1-138M-hg38", trust_remote_code=True)

DNAseq = "TGATGATTGGCGCGGCTAGGATCGGCT"
inputs = tokenizer(DNAseq, return_tensors = 'pt')["input_ids"]
hidden_states = model(inputs)[0]

embedding_max = torch.max(hidden_states[0], dim=0)[0]
print(embedding_max.shape)
PY
steps.explanation: The model card's two code blocks joined and wrapped in a shell heredoc. It downloads the tokenizer and weights, runs one forward pass and prints the pooled embedding's shape.

name: Nucleotide Transformer v3
description: Nucleotide Transformer v3 genomic language model family (pre- and post-trained checkpoints).

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: Nucleotide Transformer v3 (NTv3) is a family of DNA models from InstaDeep that read up to about 1 million bases at single-base resolution, across many species. Pre-trained checkpoints learn from unlabelled genomes by predicting masked bases and give embeddings. Post-trained checkpoints are further trained to predict functional genomics tracks (such as chromatin accessibility, histone marks and transcription factor binding) and genome annotations, given the species.
profile.summary_source_locator: docs/nucleotide_transformer_v3.md at commit 2dc37b86: opening, Model Variants and Sizes, How to Use

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: NTv3 is a U-Net. A convolutional tower shortens the single-base token sequence by 2 to the power of the number of downsampling blocks (128 for the main models, which have 7), a transformer processes the compressed sequence with self-attention, and a deconvolutional tower with skip connections restores single-base resolution. Pre-training uses masked language modelling on 9 trillion base pairs from OpenGenome2, with a length curriculum up to 1 Mb. Post-training adds supervised learning on about 16,000 functional tracks and annotation labels from 24 species, with adaptive layer norms for species conditioning. Post-trained track and annotation outputs cover the middle 37.5% of the input.
sections.source_locator: docs at commit 2dc37b86: Architecture, Training Overview, Ablations note, How to Use

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The initial release (2025) has pre-trained models of 8M, 100M and 650M parameters and post-trained models of 100M and 650M, plus intermediate checkpoints (8kb and 131kb stages) and experimental 5-downsample models of 592M. Each repository is tagged v1.0. These checkpoints need the code at commit 2dc37b8. InstaDeep has since released a second generation (NTv3_pretrained, NTv3_tracks, NTv3_tracks_1mb, NTv3_annot_mammals, _plants, _insects) with a different architecture, which the current code loads instead; the initial-release checkpoints are unchanged and still published. A result should name the checkpoint, the revision or v1.0 tag, and the code commit; this page read NTv3_100M_post at revision 28cb2afa.

steps.title: Run the post-trained model
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import jax.numpy as jnp
from nucleotide_transformer_v3.pretrained import get_posttrained_ntv3_model

# Get post-trained model
posttrained_model, tokenizer, config = get_posttrained_ntv3_model(
    model_name="NTv3_100M_post",
)

# Get data and tokenize it - 2 sequences of length 2**15 (32768 nucleotides)
seq_length = 2**15  # 32768
sequences = ["A" * seq_length, "T" * seq_length]  # 2 sequences
tokens = tokenizer.batch_np_tokenize(sequences)

# Get species token from conditions vocabulary
species = 'human'
species_tokens = posttrained_model.encode_species(species)

outs = posttrained_model(
    tokens=tokens,
    species_tokens=species_tokens,
)

logits = outs["logits"]
bigwig_logits = outs["bigwig_tracks_logits"]
bed_logits = outs["bed_tracks_logits"]

print(f"logits shape: {logits.shape}")  # Full sequence length
print(f"bigwig_logits shape: {bigwig_logits.shape}")  # Cropped to middle 37.5%
print(f"bed_logits shape: {bed_logits.shape}")  # Cropped to middle 37.5%
PY
