run_guide.summary: Pull the DeepVariant 1.10.0 Docker image, download the small test bundle and call variants in a 10 kb region of chromosome 20.
prerequisites: A Unix-like machine with the AVX instruction set and Docker (the quick start installs docker.io with apt).
No GPU needed; a GPU image exists for the call_variants step.
Network access to Docker Hub and storage.googleapis.com.
Code is BSD-3-Clause; no separate licence for the models is stated.

steps.title: Get the Docker image
steps.shell:
BIN_VERSION="1.10.0"

sudo apt -y update
sudo apt-get -y install docker.io
sudo docker pull google/deepvariant:"${BIN_VERSION}"
steps.explanation: Copied from the quick start. The models are inside the image.

steps.title: Download the test bundle
steps.shell:
INPUT_DIR="${PWD}/quickstart-testdata"
DATA_HTTP_DIR="https://storage.googleapis.com/deepvariant/quickstart-testdata"

mkdir -p ${INPUT_DIR}
wget -P ${INPUT_DIR} "${DATA_HTTP_DIR}"/NA12878_S1.chr20.10_10p1mb.bam
wget -P ${INPUT_DIR} "${DATA_HTTP_DIR}"/NA12878_S1.chr20.10_10p1mb.bam.bai
wget -P ${INPUT_DIR} "${DATA_HTTP_DIR}"/ucsc.hg19.chr20.unittest.fasta
wget -P ${INPUT_DIR} "${DATA_HTTP_DIR}"/ucsc.hg19.chr20.unittest.fasta.fai
steps.explanation: A subset of the quick start's download lines: the BAM, its index, the reference FASTA and its index, which the run step uses. The quick start also downloads truth files for evaluation with hap.py.

steps.title: Call variants
steps.shell:
OUTPUT_DIR="${PWD}/quickstart-output"
mkdir -p "${OUTPUT_DIR}"

sudo docker run \
  -v "${INPUT_DIR}":"/input" \
  -v "${OUTPUT_DIR}":"/output" \
  google/deepvariant:"${BIN_VERSION}" \
  /opt/deepvariant/bin/run_deepvariant \
  --model_type=WGS \
  --vcf_stats_report=true \
  --ref=/input/ucsc.hg19.chr20.unittest.fasta \
  --reads=/input/NA12878_S1.chr20.10_10p1mb.bam \
  --regions "chr20:10,000,000-10,010,000" \
  --output_vcf=/output/output.vcf.gz \
  --output_gvcf=/output/output.g.vcf.gz \
  --intermediate_results_dir /output/intermediate_results_dir \
  --num_shards=1
steps.explanation: Copied from the quick start. run_deepvariant runs make_examples, call_variants and postprocess_variants in turn.
steps.source_locator: deepvariant-quick-start.md: Run DeepVariant with one command

outputs: In quickstart-output: output.vcf.gz and output.g.vcf.gz with their .tbi indexes, output.visual_report.html, and the intermediate_results_dir directory.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
The example covers 10 kb of chromosome 20 with the WGS model; other data types need a different --model_type.
The test data are on hg19; this says nothing about accuracy on other builds.

profile.summary: ModernGENA is a DNA language model that adapts the ModernBERT encoder to genomic sequences. It reads DNA split into byte-pair-encoding (BPE) tokens and was pretrained by masked language modelling on 443 vertebrate genome assemblies. It outputs token embeddings that are fine-tuned for downstream tasks such as sequence classification or per-token regression; the authors present it as an efficient baseline for future DNA model work.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC abstract; model card: Tokenization, Pretraining corpus; GENA_LM examples README

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ModernGENA is a BERT-style encoder built on ModernBERT. The model card lists RoPE positional embeddings, hybrid local and global attention, pre-norm transformer blocks, GeGLU feed-forward layers and end-to-end unpadding, with FlashAttention for faster inference on compatible hardware. In the published configurations, local attention covers 128 tokens and every third layer uses global attention. Input DNA is tokenised with the 32k BPE vocabulary from GENA-LM over the symbols A, T, G, C and N. Pretraining used masked language modelling on intervals sampled from -16 kbp to +8 kbp around each transcription start site, on both strands, to reduce the weight of simple repeats.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Technical features, Tokenization, Pretraining corpus; config.json

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two checkpoints are released on Hugging Face: ModernGENA base (22 layers, hidden size 768, 12 attention heads) and ModernGENA large (28 layers, hidden size 1024, 16 attention heads). Both use the same tokenizer, the same pretraining corpus description and a vocabulary of 32768 tokens. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision; this page read base at revision 7036ebb6 and large at revision 01de8202. The paper says the full implementation and configuration are released; the fine-tuning examples the card links to live in the GENA_LM repository.

run_guide.summary: Create the ModernGENA example environment from the GENA_LM repository at a pinned commit and load a pretrained ModernGENA checkpoint with its tokenizer.
prerequisites: conda, to build the environment from examples/modernGENA/environment.yml (python>=3.10,<3.13, torch>=2.4,<2.7, transformers>=4.45,<5.0).
The loading snippet requests attn_implementation="flash_attention_2". The environment file does not install flash-attn, and the sources state no GPU type or memory.

steps.title: Load the tokenizer and a pretrained checkpoint
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("AIRI-Institute/gena-lm-bert-base-t2t")
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("AIRI-Institute/moderngena-base", trust_remote_code=True, attn_implementation="flash_attention_2")
PY
steps.explanation: The model card snippet, wrapped in a shell heredoc. It downloads the GENA-LM tokenizer and the ModernGENA base weights. For the large model, use AIRI-Institute/moderngena-large as in its card.

review.method_note: Independent review pass. Both pinned artifacts were re-downloaded and their SHA-256 checked against the source records, the mutable abstract page included, and both matched. A pdftotext -layout run (poppler 26.08.0) on the refetched PDF is byte for byte the contents of the archived gzipped text layer, so the archive is provably derived from the pinned bytes. npm run batch -- check-values reproduced the extractor's figures exactly (64 in_cell, 11 in_row, 6 locator_not_parsed, no wrong_column and no overclaimed_in_row) and wrote the same value-check.tsv. All 81 results were then re-read by review/recheck_tables.py, written for this pass and using neither extract/parse_tables.py nor extract/check_tables.py: it takes each table's column spans from the character offsets of that table's own printed header line, assigns every numeric token on a body line to the column whose header centre is nearest, and matches cells to records through each result's source_locator text rather than its ID, checking printed_value, numeric_value, the printed spread and the system the result's evaluation names. Two negative controls confirmed it fails on a swapped pair of values and on a cell shifted into the neighbouring column. A manual check of 16 cells covered column assignment in all three tables, including Table 2's unlabelled PerturbPFN score line, Table 1's third label and value pair on each of its three rows, and Table 3's middle columns. The printed overall score was re-derived as the equal-weight mean of each row's three normalised columns. The 54 descriptive records were read against Sections 2 to 5, Appendices A to E and Tables 4 to 8 of the pinned PDF.

profile.summary: Borzoi is a neural network that predicts RNA-seq coverage, the read depth along genes in different cell types and tissues, directly from DNA sequence. It takes a 524 kb stretch of human or mouse genome and outputs predicted coverage for thousands of experiments in 32 bp bins. Comparing predictions for the reference and the variant sequence gives scores for a variant's effect on gene expression, splicing and polyadenylation.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; README.md: introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Borzoi is a supervised model, not a language model: it is trained to reproduce measured coverage tracks. It uses the core Enformer architecture, a tower of convolution and pooling blocks followed by self-attention blocks at 128 bp resolution, then a U-net that upsamples back to 32 bp resolution. The training targets are RNA-seq coverage from ENCODE and GTEx plus the Enformer training data (CAGE, DNase-seq, ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq). Variant effects are computed from the difference between predicted coverage for the reference and the alternate sequence, summarised by statistics such as logSED for gene expression, COVR for polyadenylation and nDi for splicing.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Main, model description; README.md: introduction; legacy score_variants tutorial

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The published model is four replicates trained with identical data splits, each distributed as a human and a mouse .h5 weight file. The authors report that an ensemble of the four replicates generally performed better than any single replicate. A separate collection of smaller Mini Borzoi models, trained on subsets of data types or with architecture changes, is also published. The repository has legacy and latest data transforms; the legacy transforms match the manuscript. A result should say which replicates were used, whether they were averaged, and which transform was applied.

name: Caduceus
description: Self-supervised DNA language model pretrained on human genomic sequence.

attributes.source_locator: Manzo et al. Table 2 and Table 3

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: Caduceus is a family of DNA language models for long human genomic sequences. It reads DNA one base at a time, looking both upstream and downstream, and is built so that a sequence and its reverse complement are treated consistently. The pretrained models output masked-base predictions and per-base embeddings that can be fine-tuned or used as features, for example for variant effect prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; model card: Model Details; README: eQTL SNP Variant Effect Prediction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Caduceus builds on the long-range Mamba block. The authors extend it to a BiMamba component that reads a sequence in both directions, and to a MambaDNA block that is also reverse-complement (RC) equivariant. The published checkpoints have hidden dimension 256 and 16 MambaDNA layers and were pretrained as masked language models on the human reference genome. In the RC-equivariant Caduceus-PS model the hidden state is twice the width of a non-equivariant model, and the card says to run a downstream model on the hidden state and its reverse complement, or average them, to get RC-invariant outputs.
sections.source_locator: arXiv abstract; model card: Model Details; README: Using Caduceus with Hugging Face

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The README lists two pretrained checkpoints on Hugging Face. Caduceus-Ph was trained with reverse-complement data augmentation. Caduceus-PS is RC equivariant by design and needs no augmentation. Both were trained on sequences of length 131k with model size 256 and 16 layers, for 50k steps at batch size 8. A result should name the checkpoint (Ph or PS) and its Hugging Face revision; this page read PS at revision d89eeb85 and Ph at revision b0477522. The repository also holds the training code used to reproduce the paper's pretraining and fine-tuning experiments.

name: Enformer
description: Convolution and Transformer model trained to predict genomic tracks from sequences of up to about 200 kb.

attributes.source_locator: Manzo et al. Table 2 and Table 3; Tang et al. Table 1 and Methods

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: Enformer is a neural network that predicts gene expression and other genomic signals directly from DNA sequence. It reads about 200 kb of sequence and predicts 5,313 human (or 1,643 mouse) tracks, such as CAGE, DNase-seq, ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq signal, in 128 bp bins across the central 114,688 bp. Comparing predictions for reference and alternate sequences gives variant effect scores, and precomputed scores are published for common 1000 Genomes variants.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract and Methods, Model architecture; README.md: Pre-computed variant effect predictions

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Enformer is a supervised model trained to reproduce measured genomic tracks. It has three parts: seven convolutional blocks with pooling that reduce 196,608 bp to 1,536 positions of 128 bp each, eleven transformer blocks that let distant positions exchange information, and a cropping layer followed by pointwise convolutions into separate human and mouse output heads. The transformer layers use relative positional basis functions and give a receptive field that reaches elements up to 100 kb away. It was trained jointly on human and mouse data from the Basenji2 dataset, with the input extended to 196,608 bp.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model architecture and Training; Results

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One pre-trained model is published, at https://tfhub.dev/deepmind/enformer/1, with code to load its weights into the Sonnet Enformer module for fine-tuning. The README's inference example passes 393,216 bp, of which the model uses only the central 196,608 bp. Precomputed SAD and SAR variant scores on hg19 and their top 20 principal components are published for frequent 1000 Genomes variants. The paper also describes fine-tuning the model on human data. A result should state the model URL and version, whether published scores were used, and the genome build.

name: GENA-LM
description: Transformer DNA language models in BERT-base, BERT-large and BigBird variants.

attributes.source_locator: Manzo et al. Table 2 and Table 3

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: GENA-LM is a family of transformer DNA language models for reading long genomic sequences, up to 36,000 base pairs in its sparse-attention versions. It takes DNA split into variable-length tokens and returns sequence representations that are fine-tuned for tasks such as promoter, splice site, enhancer and chromatin profile prediction. Most models were trained on the human T2T genome, and species-specific and multispecies models also exist.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Materials and methods (Sequence tokenization); README_previous_generation.md: Pre-trained models, Downstream tasks

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GENA-LM models are BERT-style transformer encoders trained as masked language models. DNA is first split by a Byte-Pair Encoding tokenizer with a dictionary of 32 000 tokens, so one token covers several bases; the paper reports a median token length of 9 bp. BERT models use pre-layer normalisation. Three models reach 4096 tokens (about 36,000 bp): two use DeepSpeed sparse attention with rotary position embeddings, and bigbird-base-t2t uses the Hugging Face BigBird implementation. The paper also describes fine-tuning with a recurrent memory mechanism to process even longer segments.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sequence tokenization, Abstract; README_previous_generation.md: Pre-trained models

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository table lists eight pretrained checkpoints: five BERT models of 512 tokens (4500 bp) and three BigBird-style models of 4096 tokens (36000 bp). They differ in depth (12 or 24 layers), in the data used for the tokenizer and for training (T2T only, T2T with 1000 Genomes SNPs, or with multispecies data), and in which chromosomes were held out. The paper also names yeast, fly and Arabidopsis models. Fine-tuned checkpoints for promoters and splice sites are kept as branches of the Hugging Face repositories. A result should name the checkpoint, the branch if any, and the Hugging Face revision; this page read gena-lm-bert-base-t2t at revision 4f1352bd. The developers have since released a successor family, modernGENA, in the same repository.

name: GPN
description: Masked DNA language model; variant effects scored by single-nucleotide masking.

attributes.source_locator: Tang et al. Table 1 and Methods

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: GPN (Genomic Pretrained Network, also called GPN-SS) is a DNA language model that learns from unaligned genome sequences alone. Given a 512-bp DNA window with some positions masked, it predicts the nucleotide at each masked position. Its main use is to score genetic variants without labels: the score is the log-likelihood ratio of the alternate against the reference allele. The published model was trained on Arabidopsis thaliana and seven other Brassicales genomes.
profile.summary_source_locator: docs/models/gpn.md introduction; paper Fig. 1 caption; model card title

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GPN is a convolutional neural network, not a transformer. The masked DNA sequence is one-hot encoded with single nucleotides as tokens, then passed through 25 convolutional blocks. Each block has a dilated convolution and a feed-forward layer, with residual connections and layer normalisation; the embedding dimension stays at 512. Training is masked language modelling: 15% of positions are masked and predicted with a cross-entropy loss. To score a variant, only the variant position is masked, and the score is the log-likelihood ratio of the alternate against the reference allele. The authors down-weighted repetitive elements in the loss; the card records a repeat weight of 0.1.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Fig. 1 caption; model card: Some hparams

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The songlab-cal/gpn repository now covers four model families: GPN, GPN-MSA, PhyloGPN and GPN-Star. This page is about single-sequence GPN. Its published checkpoint is songlab/gpn-brassicales, which uses a seven-token DNA tokenizer. The same family also has an animal promoter model (songlab/gpn-animal-promoter) and a sorghum gene-expression model fine-tuned from gpn-brassicales. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision; this page read gpn-brassicales at revision eb9c35d0. The paper analyses are kept in an archive branch, and the maintained training recipe is in recipes/gpn_training. Note that the existing benchmark source (Tang et al. 2025) did not use gpn-brassicales: it evaluated a custom GPN pre-trained on the human reference genome.

strengths.text: Needs only a reference genome: the authors say the model can be applied to any species with one, without functional genomics data.
Single-nucleotide tokens make variant scoring direct: one position is masked and the two alleles compared.

limitations.text: The published checkpoint is a plant model (Arabidopsis and seven other Brassicales). For other species, a user needs another checkpoint or must train one.
The context window is 512 bp, so it sees only local sequence around a variant.
The variant scorer accepts only biallelic SNVs, and the score is raw and uncalibrated.
The authors trained each model on GPUs (about 4 days on 4 NVIDIA A100 80 GB). The sources give no minimum hardware for inference; inference defaults to FP32 on any device.

prerequisites: Python 3.13, which the package supports.

Your own inputs: a variants table (for example variants.parquet) of biallelic SNVs with one-based pos, and the matching reference genome FASTA. The published checkpoint is for Brassicales genomes.

steps.explanation: Installs the gpn package with the file-backed inference commands. The PyPI release is not pinned to the commit read here.

python - <<'PY'
from gpn import register_auto_classes
from transformers import AutoModelForMaskedLM

register_auto_classes("ss")

model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained("songlab/gpn-brassicales")
PY
steps.explanation: The GPN quick-start snippet from the documentation, wrapped in a shell heredoc. It downloads the gpn-brassicales weights and loads them as a masked language model.

steps.title: Score variants
steps.shell:
gpn ss vep \
  --input-path variants.parquet \
  --genome-path genome.fa.gz \
  --window-size 512 \
  --model-path songlab/gpn-brassicales \
  --output-path scores.parquet \
  --per-device-eval-batch-size 64

outputs: scores.parquet, with one row per input variant. Its score column is the raw, uncalibrated alternate-minus-reference log-likelihood ratio averaged over both strands; negative values mean the alternate is less likely.

name: HyenaDNA
description: DNA language model pretrained on the human reference genome with context lengths of 32 kb to 1 Mb.

attributes.source_locator: Manzo et al. Table 2 and Table 3; Tang et al. Table 1 and Methods

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: HyenaDNA is a family of DNA language models that read very long stretches of genome one base at a time, up to 1 million bases in the largest model. It was pretrained on the human reference genome by predicting the next base, and it outputs per-base embeddings that can be fine-tuned for tasks such as finding regulatory elements or classifying species.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: Intro; model card: Model & Training Overview; arXiv abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: HyenaDNA replaces attention with a stack of Hyena operators, which use input projections, implicit long convolutions and gating and scale sub-quadratically with sequence length. Each layer has a global receptive field. A single-character tokenizer with a vocabulary of the 4 nucleotides plus special tokens keeps single-base resolution. The model is causal: it is pretrained by next-nucleotide prediction on the human reference genome (HG38), and the inference script pads on the left for that reason.
sections.source_locator: model card: Model & Training Overview; huggingface.py: inference_single

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The README lists seven pretrained checkpoints of different size and training sequence length, all trained on hg38: tiny-1k, tiny-1k-d256, tiny-16k-d128, small-32k, medium-160k, medium-450k and large-1m. Each exists as a weights-only repository for the original GitHub code and as a transformers-compatible copy with an -hf suffix; the model card says the two give identical outputs. A result should name the checkpoint, which interface was used, and the revision; this page read LongSafari/hyenadna-large-1m-seqlen-hf at revision 0a629abf. A Docker image with the exact Nucleotide Transformer benchmark settings from the paper is also provided.

name: Sei
description: Supervised sequence model built from residual dilated convolutions and pretrained on 21,907 chromatin profiling datasets.

attributes.source_locator: Manzo et al. Table 2 and Table 3; Tang et al. Table 1 and Methods

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: Sei is a deep learning model that reads a 4-kb human DNA sequence and predicts the probability of 21,907 chromatin profiles (transcription factor binding, histone marks and chromatin accessibility) at its centre. Those predictions are then summarised into 40 sequence classes, such as promoter, cell type-specific enhancer or Polycomb-repressed, which give a score for a sequence or for the effect of a variant.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results (model) and Methods; README: introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The Sei model has three parts: a convolutional network with parallel linear and nonlinear paths, residual dilated convolution layers that widen the receptive field without losing resolution, and a B-spline basis layer that reduces 256 spatial bins to 16 before fully connected output layers. It was trained with Selene in PyTorch as a multi-label classifier: for each 4-kb region, the label is whether the centre base overlaps a peak in each of the 21,907 profiles. The authors then predicted 30 million genome positions at a 100-bp step, reduced the predictions with PCA and clustered them with Louvain community detection. The 40 largest clusters are the sequence classes. A sequence's class score is a projection of its chromatin predictions onto each class vector; for variants the score is alt minus ref, with histone predictions adjusted for nucleosome occupancy.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model architecture and training, Sequence classes; README: Sequence class prediction

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is one released Sei model, published on Zenodo (record 4906996, dated 2021-06-07) as a 3,281,639,255-byte archive. The repository download script fetches it, with a resources archive holding hg19 and hg38 FASTA files. Whole-genome sequence class annotations for hg38, and for hg19 lifted over from hg38, are in a separate Zenodo record, and the authors recommend these annotations over raw sequence class scores for reference genome sequences. The training configuration is in train/train.yml. A result should name the repository commit and the Zenodo model record; this page read commit 1e16bff9.

name: TREDNet
description: Two-phase CNN for enhancer prediction and variant prioritisation, developed by the group of the senior author of the comparison that evaluated it.

profile.summary: TREDNet predicts whether a 2,000 base pair stretch of human DNA acts as an enhancer, and how much a single-nucleotide variant changes that prediction. It works in two stages: a first convolutional network turns the one-hot encoded sequence into 1,924 predicted epigenomic signals (DNase I hypersensitivity, histone modifications and transcription factor binding), and a second, smaller network turns that vector into an enhancer probability for one tissue or cell line. Released phase two models cover pancreatic islets, HepG2 and K562.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results, TREDNet: A DL Model for Enhancer Prediction; README: Phase one, Phase two; Kipoi phase one model.yaml: schema

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Phase one is a multitask convolutional classifier in the style of DeepSEA, Beluga and DanQ. It takes a one-hot encoded 2,000 base window and outputs 1,924 values, one per epigenomic feature. Phase two is a smaller convolutional network trained on enhancer regions, but each region is first passed through phase one and so is represented by the 1,924-value vector rather than by its sequence. Phase two can be a single-output classifier for one tissue or a multitask classifier over several. Chromosomes 8 and 9 were held out of training and used for testing.
sections.source_locator: README: Phase one, Phase two; paper: Results; Kipoi model.yaml files: schema, info

sections.title: Scoring variants and regions
sections.body: The repository's score_variant.py reads a VCF, needs an hg19 FASTA, and writes a tab-separated file. With -score-iep it builds the 2,000 base reference and alternate sequences centred on the SNP, predicts both, and scores the variant as the larger probability times the absolute difference between the two. With -score-delta it takes the 2,000 base window around the variant, substitutes every other base at each position from 990 to 1010, averages the drop from the reference prediction at each position and divides by the median absolute value, writing the resulting list of values. Separately, the paper reports saturated mutagenesis across whole enhancers, which it calls enhancer damage (ED) scores, and defines peaks and dips in them as enhancer damaging regions (EDRs) and enhancer strengthening regions (ESRs). A second module, peak_detection/annotate.py, performs what the README calls PAS/DAS detection from a file of precomputed deltas.
sections.source_locator: README: Run the command, Run PAS/DAS detection; score_variant.py: generate_scores; paper: Figure 1 legend

sections.body: Four weight files are released on Zenodo record 6463875: one phase one model and three phase two models (islets, HepG2, K562). profile.summary: CI-SpliceAI predicts whether a DNA variant disrupts RNA splicing. It keeps the SpliceAI deep convolutional network design but retrains it on manually curated GENCODE splice sites, with all isoforms of a gene collapsed into one, and on all chromosomes. Given a VCF file and a human reference genome, it reports for each variant the predicted gain or loss of acceptor and donor sites and where they occur.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Introduction; README: Differences to SpliceAI, Output

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CI-SpliceAI uses the SpliceAI design: five deep convolutional neural networks that label every nucleotide as acceptor, donor or neither, using 10,000 nucleotides of flanking context. For training, GENCODE v37 (GRCh38) transcripts with automated (level 3) annotation were removed, and all remaining splice sites of a gene were merged into one collapsed isoform. Sequences were cut into 15,000-base windows, each predicting 5,000 central nucleotides. The training procedure was reimplemented from SpliceAI, with categorical cross-entropy and the Adam optimiser. The five trained networks are packed into one frozen graph. To score a variant, the tool predicts on the reference and the variant sequence and reports the change (delta score) for acceptor and donor gain and loss.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Methods, Splice site recognition; Algorithmic comparison on variant data; Train README: aggregate.py

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper trained the model twice: on SpliceAI's 19 training chromosomes, for a fair comparison, and on all chromosomes, which is the final model shipped in the annotation package as the frozen file CI-SpliceAI.pb. At the commit read, setup.cfg gives package version 1.2.1, while PyPI serves 1.2.2 as the latest release. A result should name the cispliceai package version and the annotation table used (grch38 by default, or grch37).

steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from cispliceai.model import CISpliceAI
from cispliceai.data import DNAPreprocessor

# you can input sequences of varying length, but it's your responsibility to ensure that the batch fits on memory!
# The sequences here are only an example, you should upload much longer slices to get sensible results

  DNAPreprocessor.onehot_and_pad('CTTCCTCTCCTCCTGCCCCACCTTCCTCTCCTCCTGCCCCACCAGAACCGGGGGCGGCTGGCAGACAAGAGGACAGTCGCCCTGCCTGCC'),

])

# Get acceptor and donor scores for the two sequences

donor_prob_1 = predictions[0][:, 2]

acceptor_prob_2 = predictions[1][:, 1]
donor_prob_2 = predictions[1][:, 2]

profile.summary: OpenSpliceAI predicts splice sites from DNA sequence. It is a PyTorch reimplementation of SpliceAI that scores every position as a donor site, an acceptor site or neither, and can also score how genetic variants change splicing. It ships a human model retrained on GRCh38 with MANE annotations, models for four other species, and tools to train new models.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction, Key Features; paper: Results

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: OpenSpliceAI keeps the SpliceAI design: a deep residual convolutional neural network that reads one-hot encoded DNA. In the 10,000 nt model the input passes through an initial Conv1D layer and 16 residual units with skip connections, then a softmax gives, for each position, the probability of donor, acceptor or neither. Smaller variants use fewer residual units (12 for 2000 nt, 8 for 400 nt). The input is padded with 5000 Ns on each side. For each flanking length five models were trained with different random seeds, and their outputs are averaged as an ensemble. The variant subcommand computes delta scores that measure how a variant changes splice site strength.
sections.source_locator: paper: Figure 1, figure supplement 1; Figure 2; Methods; README.md: What OpenSpliceAI Does

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The human model, OSAI-MANE, was released at four flanking lengths (80, 400, 2000 and 10000 nt), each as five checkpoint files (Model 1 to 5). The authors strongly recommend the 10000 nt model; the others are for experimental and research use. Species models exist for mouse, zebrafish, honey bee and thale cress. The README at the commit read shows version v.0.0.7. A result should name the species model, the flanking length, whether the five-model ensemble or a single seed was used, and the package version.

profile.summary: SpliceAI2 is a deep learning model from Illumina that predicts RNA splicing from genomic sequence. It reads about 200 kb of DNA around a gene and predicts how much each position is used as a splice donor or acceptor, how much each splice junction is used, and the most likely complete transcripts. Comparing predictions for reference and alternate alleles gives a score for how strongly a variant changes splicing.
profile.summary_source_locator: Manuscript: Main 'Hierarchical model of RNA splicing'; Methods 'Variant effect prediction'; README: introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The input is 196,608 bp of genomic sequence on the gene's sense strand, one-hot encoded, plus a one-hot code for the species (ten channels). A dense layer projects it to 256 channels, and 20 MetaFormer blocks follow, each with a depth-wise dilated convolution and a feed-forward network, at progressively coarser pooling. Each block's output feeds a splice site head over the central 65,536 positions. The 1,024 positions with the highest splice site usage are then paired by a query-key product to give a 1,024 by 1,024 matrix of splice junction usage. Sites and junctions form a splice graph, and Viterbi decoding finds the highest scoring paths, which are the predicted transcripts. The model was trained end-to-end on splice site, junction and transcript usage, with the three losses summed.
sections.source_locator: Manuscript: Methods 'SpliceAI2 model' (Inputs, Architecture, Outputs, Training); 'Transcript prediction'

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The code is package version 2.0 (this page read commit 1dcd2a18 on main). The released model is an ensemble of two checkpoints trained with identical settings, held on Hugging Face as spliceai2_multispecies_13M_01 and spliceai2_multispecies_13M_02, each with a model.ckpt; the README's commands pass both folders. Illumina also publishes precomputed scores for all possible single nucleotide variants and observed indels in protein-coding genes (GENCODE v48, GRCh38). The manuscript also describes a tissue-specific model conditioned on RBP expression; the files read do not show it as released. A result should name the package version, both checkpoint folders and the Hugging Face revision (55948bae read here).

strengths.text: It predicts splice junctions and whole transcripts as well as splice sites, so a variant's effect can be read as a change in transcript structure, not only a site score.
Long context: each prediction sees 196,608 bp of sequence.
Precomputed scores cover all possible single nucleotide variants and observed indels in human protein-coding genes, and the output keeps SpliceAI-compatible columns and threshold equivalents.
The authors report improved detection of splice-altering variants and better quantification of their effects across cryptic splicing, sQTL and MPRA benchmarks; this is their claim.

limitations.text: Restrictive licence: non-commercial organisations only, no redistribution, no use to train other models, research use only and not for diagnostic procedures. This applies to the code as well as the weights.
A CUDA-capable GPU is required.
Weights are gated on Hugging Face and need a manual access request with academic details.
The user must supply the gene strand for each variant; if it is unknown, both strands have to be scored and combined.

profile.summary: GPN-Promoter (Hugging Face name gpn-animal-promoter) is a DNA language model trained on promoter sequences from animal genomes. It was released with TraitGym, a benchmark of causal regulatory variants in human genetics. Given a DNA window, it predicts masked nucleotides; the GPN tools turn this into a variant score, the log-likelihood ratio of the alternate against the reference allele, or into sequence embeddings.
profile.summary_source_locator: docs/models/gpn.md: Animal promoter model and TraitGym; TraitGym README: Code; model card: Basic usage; docs/getting-started/cli.md: GPN

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GPN-Promoter belongs to the GPN (GPN-SS) family: single-sequence genomic language models trained on unaligned genomes with masked language modelling. The published config uses the GPN model type with a ByteNet-style convolutional encoder of 64 layers and hidden size 1024, a first kernel size of 9 and later kernel size of 5, with dilation base 2 cycling every 8 layers. The vocabulary has 7 tokens, from the tokenizer gonzalobenegas/tokenizer-dna-mlm named in the training script. The archived training command used a dataset version called v6/512, 64 layers and hidden size 1024, with a total batch size of 2048. For variant scoring, the GPN package compares the model's likelihood of the alternate and reference alleles, averaged over both strands.
sections.source_locator: docs/models/gpn.md; config.json; archived train.sh and README.md; docs/getting-started/cli.md

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility

Intermediate training checkpoints from the same run are in a separate Hugging Face dataset, and the training data are in songlab/gpn-animal-promoter-dataset. The analysis code that produced the model is preserved under the ref analysis-archive-2026-08-18 of the GPN repository. The model card imports gpn.model, while the current GPN docs (commit dc5fd287 read here) load GPN models through register_auto_classes("ss"). profile.summary: FramePool predicts how strongly a 5' untranslated region (5' UTR) drives translation, measured as mean ribosome load, directly from the 5' UTR sequence. It is a convolutional network trained on a massively parallel reporter assay, made to accept 5' UTRs of any length by pooling motif detections separately in each of the three reading frames. Through Kipoi, it takes variants from a VCF file and reports the predicted log2 fold change in mean ribosome load for each affected 5' UTR.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; README; Kipoi model.yaml: info.doc

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: FramePool adapts the published MPRA model of Sample et al. That model used a dense layer, so it only worked for the sequence lengths it was trained on. FramePool keeps three convolutional layers (kernel size 7, 128 filters each, with residual skip connections) and replaces the position-specific dense input with global max and average pooling, done separately for each of the three frames relative to the start codon. The pooled values (a vector of 768) go into a dense layer of 64 neurons and a final linear output. Each model has 282,625 learnable weights; the combined model has 4 more in a scaling layer. The model was trained with the Adam optimiser and a mean squared error loss.
sections.source_locator: README; Paper: Methods, Framepool model; Model training

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper trains three models: FramePool50 on 50-nucleotide MPRA sequences, FramePool100 on 25 to 100 nucleotide sequences, and FramePoolCombined on both, with a scaling layer for the two libraries. The paper names FramePoolCombined as the model for variant effect prediction from VCF files. The Kipoi zoo entry downloads the weights file Framepool_combined_residual.h5 from Zenodo record 3584238 with a fixed md5 checksum. A result should name the Kipoi model (Framepool), the weights checksum and the kipoi/models commit; this page read commit 770dcaf2.

limitations.text: Cannot reliably detect upstream open reading frames longer than 19 nucleotides, and cannot model the order of upstream start sites, so leaky scanning is only partly captured.
Trained on reporter assay data from one cell line (HEK293T, eGFP library), so it predicts the effect of 5' UTR sequence only, without coding sequence or 3' UTR context.
The Kipoi environment pins an old stack: Python 3.7, TensorFlow 1.13.1, Keras 2.2.4 and h5py 2.9.0.

Variant scoring through Kipoi expects a single-sample VCF: the BED and VCF must be sorted with a tabix index, chromosome naming must match across files, and a VCF that mixes patients gives results that are not meaningful.

run_guide.summary: Install Kipoi, create the Framepool environment, and score the example variants with the Kipoi command line, as shown on the Kipoi model page.
prerequisites: conda (anaconda or miniconda), which Kipoi uses to manage model dependencies. Kipoi maintains Python 3.6 to 3.10.
For Python 3.8 to 3.10, the Kipoi README says hdf5 and pkgconfig must be installed before Kipoi.
The Framepool environment itself pins Python 3.7, TensorFlow 1.13.1 and Keras 2.2.4. A GPU is not mentioned.
Code and weights are MIT licensed.

  --dataloader_args='{"intervals_file": "example/intervals_file", "fasta_file": "example/fasta_file", "vcf_file": "example/vcf_file", "vcf_file_tbi": "example/vcf_file_tbi", "chr_order_file": "example/chr_order_file", "num_chr": true}' \

profile.summary: The Jores plant promoter CNN is a pair of convolutional neural networks that predict how strongly a plant core promoter drives gene expression. Each model takes a 170-base promoter sequence (from 165 bases upstream to 5 bases downstream of the transcription start site) and outputs a single number, the promoter strength measured by STARR-seq. One model was trained on measurements in tobacco leaves and the other on maize protoplasts, using promoters from Arabidopsis, maize and sorghum.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results, Computational modelling of promoter strength; Methods, Library design and construction; notebook: Build the models; README: folders

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The sequence is one-hot encoded and passed to two forward- and reverse-strand scan layers, adapted from DeepGMAP, with 128 filters of width 13. These feed a standard convolutional layer (128 filters, width 13, ReLU). Each convolutional layer is followed by dropout at rate 0.15. A dense layer of 64 units with batch normalisation and ReLU leads to a final dense layer with one output. The first convolutional kernel is initialised with clustered transcription factor and core promoter element motifs. The models are trained as regressions with mean squared error loss on the measured enrichment, with Adam, early stopping and learning-rate reduction.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Computational modelling of promoter strength; notebook: Build the models

sections.title: Use for promoter design
sections.body: The authors used the models for in silico evolution. In each round, every single-nucleotide variant of a promoter is scored and the best is kept for the next round. Scoring can use the tobacco model, the maize model, or the mean of both. The authors synthesised and tested promoters after three and ten rounds. They report a large rise in measured strength after three rounds and a smaller further rise after ten, and that the averaged score gave promoters active in both systems.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Computational modelling of promoter strength; Methods, In silico evolution of promoter sequences

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two trained models are committed to the repository as TensorFlow SavedModel folders: CNN/model_leaf (tobacco leaf) and CNN/model_proto (maize protoplast). The training and test tables used are in the same folder. The notebook loads a saved model if its folder exists and trains a new one otherwise. A result should name the model (leaf or proto) and the repository commit; this page read commit ace4ead5.

limitations.text: Input is fixed at 170 bases of core promoter. The models do not see distal enhancers, 5' UTRs or longer regulatory context.

The repository declares no licence, so reuse terms for the code and models are unclear.
The repository has no install instructions or environment file. The paper names TensorFlow 2.2 only.

profile.summary: Optimus 5-Prime is a convolutional neural network that predicts how well a 5' UTR sequence drives translation, measured as mean ribosome load (MRL). It reads a one-hot encoded 5' UTR, 50 nucleotides in the main model, and outputs a single MRL value. It was trained on polysome profiling of 280,000 random 5' UTRs placed in front of an eGFP reporter, and the authors also used it with a genetic algorithm to design new 5' UTRs.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, Modeling 5' UTRs and ribosome loading; Fig. 2 legend

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The authors built a library of 280,000 reporter constructs with random 5' UTRs and a constant eGFP coding sequence and 3' UTR, measured ribosome loading by polysome profiling and RNA sequencing, and trained a CNN on 260,000 of them, holding out 20,000 for testing. The chosen architecture, from a 10-fold cross-validated grid search, has three convolution layers of 120 filters with filter length 8 and ReLU activation, a 40-node dense layer with 20% dropout, and one linear output. It was written in Python 2.7 with Keras on a TensorFlow backend and trained for three epochs. A separate model with the same layout predicts the full polysome profile, and a generalised version reads 5' UTRs of 25 to 100 nucleotides, zero-padded to 100.
sections.source_locator: Paper: MPRA design and validation; Online Methods, Convolution Neural Network, Polysome Profile Model, Generalized CNN

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository holds several saved Keras models in modeling/saved_models: the main MRL model (Figure 2), a retrained main model (Figure 4), a model for the genetic algorithm and its retrained version, and the polysome distribution model. The same folder also holds Varying_length_25to100_model.hdf5, whose name matches the paper's generalised 25 to 100 nucleotide model. Six further .h5 models (e1, e2, ep1, ep2, emp1, emp2) sit in modeling/cds_modification_comparisons/saved_data; the paper describes models trained on chemically modified RNA, but the sources read do not explain these file names. A result should name the saved .hdf5 file and the commit; this page read commit d53df410. Training data are on GEO (GSE114002).

profile.summary: GPN-Star is a DNA language model that predicts how strongly each position of a genome is constrained by evolution, and so how damaging a single-nucleotide variant there is likely to be. It reads a window of a whole-genome alignment of many species with their species tree, predicts masked nucleotides of the target genome, and scores a variant by how much less likely the alternate allele is than the reference. Human models exist at vertebrate, mammal and primate timescales, and further models cover five model organisms.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract and Main; docs/models/gpn-star.md: opening paragraph and Models; cli.md: GPN section on the output score

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GPN-Star is an encoder-only Transformer trained to predict masked nucleotides. Each input is a window of a whole-genome alignment and its species tree. The alignment is split into target sequences and source sequences. Source species that are closely related are pooled into clade-level representations. Each encoder block has self-attention along the target sequence, a phylogeny-informed cross-attention module that reads the source sequences weighted by evolutionary distances from the species tree, and a feed-forward network. The published vertebrate human checkpoint has 16 layers, hidden size 1024 and 16 attention heads.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Main, Fig. 1 legend and model description; config.json

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Eight checkpoints are published. Three are human (hg38) models of 200M parameters each, trained on a 100-way vertebrate, a 447-way mammalian and a 243-way primate alignment; the paper calls them GPN-Star (V), (M) and (P). Five are for model organisms: mouse and chicken (85M parameters), fly (85M), worm and arabidopsis (25M). Each checkpoint needs the alignment it was trained on, with matching assembly, species set, species order and evolutionary scale. Genome-wide scores are published, so many uses need no inference. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision, whether published scores or new inference were used, and the window size.

strengths.text: Genome-wide scores are published for the human genome and the five model organisms, so variants can be looked up without running the model.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Data availability; docs/models/gpn-star.md: Alignments and scores

strengths.text: Training cost is modest by the authors' account: the 200 million parameter models were trained for several days on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs.

Separate human models at three evolutionary timescales let a user choose; the authors report that deeper timescales better capture coding and highly constrained regions, and shallower ones better inform fast-evolving regulatory elements.
Code and weights are MIT licensed, and the package supports both inference and training on prepared alignments.
strengths.source_locator: README.md; Hugging Face API response; docs/models/gpn-star.md: opening paragraph

limitations.text: Inference needs a whole-genome alignment that matches the checkpoint. The human vertebrate archive is about 42 GB compressed, more once extracted, and the command-line tool does not download it.
Variant scoring covers biallelic single-nucleotide variants. The authors say the fixed alignment format makes the model less suited to indels and structural variants.
Scores from the command-line tool are raw and uncalibrated. The paper's results use mutation-rate calibrated scores, so raw output is not directly comparable to them.
The model is trained on DNA sequence alone and is not specific to any tissue.

run_guide.summary: Install the gpn package, load the vertebrate human checkpoint, download and arrange its alignment, and score variants from the command line.
prerequisites: For many uses no run is needed: genome-wide scores are published at https://huggingface.co/datasets/songlab/gpn-star-scores.
Python with pip. The repository badge names Python 3.13.
Disk space for the vertebrate alignment archive: about 42 GB compressed, plus more for the extracted Zarr store. The hf, sha256sum and unpigz commands are used to fetch and unpack it.

Variants as biallelic single-nucleotide variants with one-based positions. The GPN-Star section of the command-line guide does not list accepted file formats; the GPN-MSA section lists Parquet, CSV/TSV, VCF, GTF and GFF.

steps.title: Install the package with inference dependencies
steps.shell: pip install "gpn[inference]"
steps.explanation: The inference extra is required for the file-backed commands.

steps.title: Load the checkpoint in Python
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from gpn import register_auto_classes
from transformers import AutoModelForMaskedLM

register_auto_classes("star")
model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained("songlab/gpn-star-hg38-v100-200m")
PY
steps.explanation: The documentation's quick start, wrapped in a shell heredoc. It downloads the weights from Hugging Face.

steps.title: Download and verify the vertebrate alignment
steps.shell:
hf download songlab/multiz100way-pigz 99.zarr.tar.gz \
  --repo-type dataset \
  --revision 6a9d42a35e7debbba845979dea6064f14d5cb3f9 \
  --local-dir .

echo '4dad7da04db9c804032c0c4c7bbefea58f694fc911e962d28c8df87f356ce4ad  99.zarr.tar.gz' \
  | sha256sum --check
unpigz --stdout 99.zarr.tar.gz | tar -xf -
steps.explanation: Copied from the documentation. The archive extracts as 99.zarr.

steps.title: Arrange the alignment store
steps.shell:
mkdir -p /path/to/multiz100way/100
mv 99.zarr /path/to/multiz100way/100/all.zarr
steps.explanation: These two lines are written by Rewire from the documentation's prose, which asks for the extracted store to be moved or symlinked to /path/to/multiz100way/100/all.zarr; the directory name 100 is significant. Replace /path/to with a real location.

steps.title: Score variants
steps.shell:
gpn star vep \
  --input-path INPUT_PATH \
  --msa-path /path/to/multiz100way \
  --window-size WINDOW_SIZE \
  --model-path songlab/gpn-star-hg38-v100-200m \
  --output-path OUTPUT_PATH
steps.explanation: The command template from the command-line guide, with the alignment path and the model name from the documentation filled in by Rewire. Replace INPUT_PATH with a variant file, WINDOW_SIZE with an even number and OUTPUT_PATH with a Parquet file name. The sources read do not give the window size for this checkpoint. Chromosome names must match the store, and the reference allele must match the alignment or inference stops.

profile.summary: LOL-EVE (Language Of Life for Evolutionary Variant Effects) scores the effect of insertions and deletions (indels) in human gene promoters without task-specific training. It is a conditional autoregressive transformer trained on 13.6 million mammalian promoter sequences, each tagged with its gene, species and clade. A variant is scored by comparing how likely the model finds the reference and the variant promoter sequence.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: Abstract; Using Hugging Face Model. Model card: Key Features

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LOL-EVE is a causal language model based on the CTRL architecture, with 12 transformer layers, hidden size 768 and 12 attention heads. Each input starts with control codes for the gene, species and clade, followed by the promoter DNA between [SOS] and [EOS] tokens; training sequences were up to 1000 base pairs. The developers describe adaptive local position embeddings and say the model uses pretrained ESM protein embeddings for gene context. To score a variant, the reference and variant sequences are each run through the model with the same control codes, the summed cross-entropy of each is computed, and the score is the variant's minus the reference's, with higher meaning more deleterious.
sections.source_locator: README: Model Specifications; Input Format; Using Hugging Face Model. Model card: Training Data

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint is published, Marks-lab/LOL-EVE on Hugging Face; this page read revision 397bbb87. Its custom model code describes itself as a simplified wrapper that builds a standard CTRL language model with the configured sizes, and its comments say that in practice this would load the actual trained model. The wrapper does not refer to ESM embeddings or adaptive position embeddings. The repository's example_usage.py uses the same wrapper and only prints the shape of the output logits. The repository's own scoring script takes a local checkpoint, tokeniser, genome and embedding file instead. A result should state which route was used (the Hugging Face wrapper or the repository script), the Hugging Face revision, and the control codes given. The paper is the MLCB 2025 work; the model card links a bioRxiv preprint and says the link is to be updated.

strengths.text: Aimed at indels in promoters, a variant class the developers say current methods handle poorly, and scores them zero-shot from sequence likelihood.
Conditions on gene, species and clade through control codes, so the same sequence can be scored in its gene and species context.
Released with three promoter indel benchmark datasets (ultra-rare variants, causal eQTLs, TFBS disruption) and the PromoterZoo training data on Hugging Face.

limitations.text: The Hugging Face model code calls itself a simplified demonstration wrapper around a standard CTRL model and does not use the ESM gene embeddings or adaptive position embeddings the README describes, so results from it may not match the paper's model.
Covers promoter windows of up to 1000 base pairs (1,007 tokens) only; it is a region-specific model, not a genome-wide one.

steps.title: Score example variants
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM
import torch
import pandas as pd

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('Marks-lab/LOL-EVE')
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained('Marks-lab/LOL-EVE', trust_remote_code=True)

def score_variants_hf(variants_df, gene, species, clade):
    scores = []
    for _, row in variants_df.iterrows():
        ref_seq = f"{gene} {species} {clade} [SOS] {row['sequence']} [EOS]"
        var_seq = f"{gene} {species} {clade} [SOS] {row['variant_sequence']} [EOS]"
        ref_inputs = tokenizer(ref_seq, return_tensors="pt")
        var_inputs = tokenizer(var_seq, return_tensors="pt")
        with torch.no_grad():
            ref_outputs = model(**ref_inputs)
            var_outputs = model(**var_inputs)
            ref_logits = ref_outputs.logits[0, :-1]
            var_logits = var_outputs.logits[0, :-1]
            ref_tokens = ref_inputs['input_ids'][0, 1:]
            var_tokens = var_inputs['input_ids'][0, 1:]
            ref_score = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(ref_logits, ref_tokens, reduction='sum')
            var_score = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(var_logits, var_tokens, reduction='sum')
            score = (var_score - ref_score).item()
            scores.append(score)
    variants_df['score'] = scores
    return variants_df

variants = pd.DataFrame({
    'sequence': ['ATGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTA', 'ATGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTA'],
    'variant_sequence': ['ATGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTA', 'ATGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTA']
})

scored_variants = score_variants_hf(variants, gene='brca1', species='human', clade='primate')
print(scored_variants)
PY
steps.explanation: The README's Hugging Face scoring example wrapped in a shell heredoc, with the docstring and comments removed. The example's variant sequences are the same as the references; replace them with real reference and variant promoter sequences.
steps.source_locator: README: Score Variants, Using Hugging Face Model

outputs: The input table printed with an added 'score' column: variant minus reference summed cross-entropy, where higher is more deleterious.

name: PromoterAI
description: Deep learning model that predicts the impact of promoter variants on gene expression. Scores range from -1 to 1 (negative for under-expression, positive for over-expression); the README recommends thresholds of 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5 in absolute value. Supports single nucleotide variants and left-normalised indels.

profile.summary: PromoterAI is a deep learning model from Illumina that predicts how a variant in a gene promoter changes that gene's expression. It takes a list of variants (chromosome, position, reference and alternative allele, strand) and a reference genome, and adds a score between -1 and 1 to each variant: negative values mean lower expression and positive values mean higher expression. The authors built it to find noncoding promoter variants that may explain rare genetic diseases.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction and Variant effect prediction; Europe PMC abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: PromoterAI is a convolutional network written in TensorFlow and Keras. The code first projects one-hot DNA (4 channels) with a 1-wide convolution, then stacks blocks that each apply a dilated depthwise convolution and a two-layer dense step, with batch normalisation and residual connections. The README's training command uses 24 blocks of width 1024, a 20,480-base input and a 4,096-base output. The model is first trained to predict regulatory profiles stored as bigWig tracks around transcription start sites, optionally across several species, and is then fine-tuned on a GTEx variant file. For variant scoring, a twin wrapper runs the model on the reference and the alternative sequence and averages the difference between the two predictions.
sections.source_locator: promoterai/architecture.py; README.md: Model training and fine-tuning; setup.py; issue 3 collaborator reply

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The Python package is at version 1.0rc6 in the repository read here. In June 2025 the authors said they had released the code and precomputed scores but not the model weights. In September 2025, answering an issue titled 'Pretrained model weights release', they said the download link is sent by email after the licence agreement linked from the README is completed. The sources read do not name or version the distributed weights, so a result should name the package version, the repository commit, the model folder used and the input length (the README uses 20480).
sections.source_locator: setup.py; issue 3 and issue 10 collaborator replies; README.md: Variant effect prediction

sections.title: Scores and thresholds
sections.body: Scores run from -1 to 1. The README recommends cut-offs at 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5 in absolute value. Because a promoter variant acts through one gene's strand, each variant row needs a strand; if it is unknown, the README says to score both strands as separate rows and combine the results. Precomputed scores for all human promoter single nucleotide variants are available for academic and non-commercial research after the licence agreement.

strengths.text: Works from plain variant coordinates and a reference genome, and handles both single nucleotide variants and left-normalised indels.
Gives a signed score, so a user can tell predicted loss of expression from predicted gain, and the README gives thresholds to apply.

The authors report that variants it flags show outlier RNA and protein expression and strong negative selection, and that they confirmed effects with reporter assays (the authors' claims, from the paper abstract).
Training, preprocessing and fine-tuning code is included, along with the benchmark and training annotation files, so the model can be retrained.
strengths.source_locator: README.md: Model training and fine-tuning; issue 3 collaborator reply

limitations.text: Not open source: the code is under the PolyForm Strict licence (noncommercial, no distribution, no derivative works), and commercial use of scores and models must be bought from Illumina.
The weights are not downloadable directly. They are sent by email after a licence agreement, and the scoring command cannot run without a model folder.
limitations.source_locator: issue 10 collaborator reply; README.md: Variant effect prediction

limitations.text: Each variant needs a strand. If the strand is unknown the user must score both strands and combine the results themselves.
Tied to TensorFlow 2.13 to 2.15 and Keras 2; GPU testing covers H100 and A100 only.

run_guide.summary: Install PromoterAI and score a small variant file against a reference genome, using a model folder obtained under the licence agreement.
prerequisites: Python 3.8 or later, with TensorFlow 2.13 to 2.15 and Keras 2 (installed by pip).
CPU or GPU; tested on H100 and A100 GPUs.
A trained PromoterAI model folder, sent by email after completing the licence agreement linked from the README. Noncommercial use only under the PolyForm Strict licence.
A reference genome FASTA file matching the variant coordinates.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/Illumina/PromoterAI
cd PromoterAI
git checkout --detach ce9fcd080556d7e962a5946327fe8fd1a04e272b
steps.explanation: Clones the official repository. The checkout line, added here, pins the commit this page was written from.

steps.title: Install
steps.shell: pip install -e .
steps.explanation: Installs the package and the promoterai command. For scoring only, the README also allows pip install promoterai.

steps.title: Prepare a variant file
steps.shell:
printf 'chrom	pos	ref	alt	strand
chr16	84145214	G	T	1
chr2	55232249	T	G	-1
' > variants.tsv
steps.explanation: Writes two of the README's example variants to a tab-separated file with the required columns. Coordinates must match the reference FASTA used in the next step.

steps.title: Score the variants
steps.shell:
promoterai \
    --model_folder path/to/model \
    --var_file variants.tsv \
    --fasta_file path/to/genome_fa \
    --input_length 20480
steps.explanation: Runs the scoring command from the README. Replace path/to/model with the model folder received under the licence agreement and path/to/genome_fa with the reference FASTA.

outputs: A copy of the variant file with a new score column, named by appending the model folder name to the variant file name.
